Span start 1.0% against 0.5% uniform-pointer chance. All three choice gates report passed=False.
impact: Three independently-seeded models landing on the identical held-out number is not noise, it is majority-class collapse: each learned to answer `stub` everywhere. That is a cleaner negative than the 4096 run's -1.4% with 8.8% spread, and it redirects the next move. Context is NOT the binding constraint, so raising it further is measurement already taken. What remains untested is model capacity (128 wide, 2 layers, ~600K parameters) and corpus size (763 training decisions from 133 files of one repository).
workaround: None needed for the measurement; --context-bytes and --examples/--manifest-in make both levers cheap to sweep. The corpus generation needs the qd-mutate Rust binary and the training needs a GPU, and those were separated for exactly this reason: the 8192 run took 111s per seed on the GH200 against an estimated 52 minutes per seed on this Mac.
action_required: A plan decision, informed now rather than guessed: rung 0's WIDTH and DEPTH, and whether the corpus should come from more than this repository. Both are one flag and one rerun. Explicitly NOT recommended: more context, which this run tested and which changed nothing.

question: GAP-RUNG0-CONTEXT-IS-NOT-THE-BINDING-CONSTRAINT settled that context does not help and named model capacity as the remaining untested lever -- which is also what docs/lappi.md calls 'the first thing to raise if rung 0 underperforms'. Does capacity help?
answer: NO. Swept 128x2 (1.52M params) -> 256x4 (5.48M) -> 512x6 (23.8M) at 8192 bytes, 3 seeds each. Mean over the majority-class baseline: +0.0%, -1.2%, -0.3%. 15.6x the parameters moved the held-out number by nothing, and the larger models converge ON the baseline rather than above it.
evidence: AUDIT/rung0-capacity-sweep-2026-09-20.json holds every point. The signature is majority-class collapse: at 128x2/8192 all three seeds scored 0.5215 to four decimals -- 158 of 303 rows, the exact size of the `stub` class -- so each model answers `stub` on every held-out row. Span accuracy stayed at 0.7-1.7% against 0.5% uniform-pointer chance at every point in the sweep. GH200, 111s to 790s per seed depending on size.
impact: docs/lappi.md's stated remedy is now measured and does not work at this corpus size. Two of the three levers the plan names are closed: context (413/161 -> 763/303 decisions bought a variance improvement and no accuracy) and capacity (15.6x parameters bought nothing). Anyone who raises either again is repeating a measurement rather than making one.
workaround: STATED CAVEAT, because it weakens one point rather than the conclusion: the 512x6 run is plausibly undertrained rather than saturated -- its final training loss is ~5.3 against ~1.7 at 256x4 and ~0.97 at 128x2, so 960 steps does not fit the training set at that size. Its held-out number is therefore weaker evidence than the 128x2 and 256x4 points, which DID fit their training data and still did not transfer. A longer schedule at 512x6 is the one cheap follow-up this sweep leaves.
action_required: The remaining lever is the CORPUS, and it is a plan decision: 763 training decisions from 133 files of one repository, gold distribution stub 51.5% / logic 30.0% / cosmetic 16.7% / clean 1.7%. Rung 0's published evidence (cua-s1-forms) is a 224-byte context over a 55-concept catalogue, and lappi.md already says 'nothing here claims 600K parameters covers' the wider problem. This sweep is the measurement that turns that caveat into a number.

tool: tools/rung0_real_run.py --train-subsample, with train-set accuracy and label_entropy
question: Three configurations landed exactly on the majority-class baseline on held-out files. Two readings are possible and they call for opposite fixes: a model that FITS its training data and cannot transfer needs a better corpus, and a model that does not fit its training data has not learned at all. Which is it?
answer: IT NEVER FITS. The model answers the majority class on every row it is ever shown, training rows included. Measured train accuracy equals the training set's own majority share to three decimals at both ends of the learning curve: 44.2% against a 44.2% `stub` share at the 25% point, 48.0% against 48.0% at 100%. This SUPERSEDES the earlier statement in this session that rung 0 'fits the training files and does not transfer', which was inferred from a falling total loss rather than measured -- train accuracy was not being measured at all until this run added it.
evidence: AUDIT/rung0-learning-curve-2026-09-20.json. The mechanism is exact: the choice channel converges to 1.128 nats against a label-distribution entropy of 1.1300 -- a gap of -0.002, which is the loss of a head that has learned the class prior and nothing conditional on the context. The TOTAL loss falls 14.546 -> 1.438 over the same run and reads as healthy training, because the span channel starts at 12.520 against the choice channel's 2.026 and supplies 86% of the initial total. The headline curve is the span channel's curve.
impact: The recommendation flips. 'More or better corpus' was the standing next step and it is now ruled out by measurement: the learning curve is flat because a corpus lever cannot move a model that is not fitting the corpus it already has. 4x the training files (181 -> 763 decisions) changed the held-out number by 0.0% and the train number not at all. The question is now why a 1.5M-parameter model cannot fit 181 examples.
workaround: The instrument is added rather than the diagnosis guessed: label_entropy over the training decisions, and a choice_loss_below_the_class_prior metric that requires the loss to sit at least 0.01 nats BELOW the floor. It records passed=false on this run with the gap spelled out. tools/rung0_toy_run.py already computed the same floor per context group -- 'the difference between a curve that moved and a head that is wired to the right rows' -- and the real run was missing it, which is why three sessions of runs read as inconclusive rather than as a head at its floor.
action_required: OPEN, and it is now a debugging question rather than a plan decision. Candidates, none yet tested: the span channel outweighing the choice channel 6:1 in an unweighted sum; mean-pooling an 8192-byte context into 128 dimensions; a learning rate of 3e-3 chosen for a toy batch. The toy run passes because it memorises a single batch, which is exactly the case this failure does not touch.

question: Every rung 0 report so far, including this repository's own, quotes a total loss. Does the total describe the run?
answer: NO, it describes the span channel. At initialisation the span loss is 12.520 and the choice loss 2.026 -- a 6.2:1 ratio, so span is 86% of the total. The total falling 14.546 -> 1.438 is almost entirely span falling 12.520 -> 0.310, while the choice head moves 2.026 -> 1.128 and stops at its prior floor.
evidence: Measured on the GH200, 8192-byte context, 25% subsample: 'total 14.5460 -> 1.4382 [choice 2.026->1.128 span 12.520->0.310]'. The two channels were already logged by Rung0Result and were never printed or recorded.
impact: This is the repository's recurring defect class -- one name, two quantities -- in the number every rung 0 run is judged by. A reader watching the total sees a 90% reduction and concludes the model is learning. Span accuracy over the same run is 0.7-1.7% against 0.5% chance, so neither head is actually working.
workaround: Both channels are now printed per seed with the choice floor beside them, and the choice channel has its own gate. The span channel still has no floor of its own recorded -- its trivial answer is known (uniform-pointer chance, reported as 0.5%) but the LOSS floor for a pointer over a variable candidate count is not computed, so the span loss is still a number without a bar.
action_required: The span channel's loss floor is the remaining uninstrumented quantity. Its accuracy is already scored against chance; its loss is not.

question: GAP-RUNG0-CHOICE-HEAD-CONVERGES-TO-THE-CLASS-PRIOR left two explanations with opposite fixes: the signal IS in the context and ByteDecider cannot extract it (architecture), or the signal is not there at this corpus size (corpus). The model under test produces the same number either way. Which is it?
answer: THE SIGNAL IS THERE. A multinomial logistic regression on hashed char n-grams, reading exactly the bytes the model reads, scores 57.4% on the same held-out FILES against a 52.1% majority-class baseline -- **+5.3%**. ByteDecider on the same split scores 52.1%, which is +0.0%. The weakest reasonable model finds class information that a 1.5M-parameter transformer does not.
evidence: Ledger row 2988ac80 (chain verifies at 171). LinearBaseline converged in 1392 iterations at l2=1e-4; train accuracy 57.3% against held-out 57.4%, so the control is not overfitting either -- it has found a modest signal that generalises. It predicts two of four classes on validation (stub 257, logic 46), so even the control is conservative and 57.4% is a floor on the extractable signal rather than a ceiling.
impact: This is the finding that redirects rung 0. Three levers were closed by measurement -- context, capacity to 15.6x parameters, corpus size -- and each closure narrowed the question without answering it. This answers it: rung 0's failure is an ARCHITECTURE or OPTIMISATION problem, and the corpus is exonerated. It also means the ladder's rung 0 result so far is not evidence that byte-level System-1 models cannot do this task.
workaround: The control was itself refused first, which is worth recording: at LinearBaseline's default of 500 iterations the fit stops at a gradient norm of 4.883e-04 against a 1e-04 tolerance, and convergence() returned NotRun -- 'an unconverged control cannot be beaten'. The ITERATION BUDGET was raised to 6000 and the TOLERANCE left alone, because the tolerance is what makes the control worth beating. Had the tolerance been loosened instead, the control would have 'converged' at a worse fit and the +5.3% would have been smaller or absent.
action_required: OPEN, and now specific. Untested candidates, in the order the evidence suggests: (1) the span channel outweighs the choice channel 6.2:1 in an unweighted sum, so the optimiser serves the pointer; (2) mean-pooling an 8192-byte context into 128 dimensions may destroy the n-gram evidence the linear model uses; (3) lr=3e-3 was chosen for a memorisable toy batch. Each is one flag and one 111-second rerun on the GH200.

question: GAP-RUNG0-A-LINEAR-CONTROL-BEATS-THE-MODEL established that the signal is in the context and ByteDecider was not extracting it, and named three untested candidates. The first was the objective: Rung0Step sums the choice and span losses unweighted, and the two channels open at 2.026 and 12.520 -- 6.2:1. Does that ratio explain the failure?
answer: YES, and the train-accuracy column is the proof rather than the held-out one. At span_weight >= 0.5 rung 0's choice accuracy on the rows it was OPTIMISED ON sits at exactly 48.0%, the training set's own majority share, on every seed -- the head emits one class and never fitted anything. Below 0.2 it breaks free to 54-77%. The collapse threshold is between 0.2 and 0.5, and the default every previous run used was 1.0, well inside the collapsed regime.
evidence: AUDIT/rung0-span-weight-2026-09-20.json. Held out, at span_weight=0.05 all five seeds beat the majority-class baseline -- 53.8/54.5/57.1/58.7/61.7% against 52.1% -- for a mean of +5.0%. That MATCHES the linear control's +5.3% rather than exceeding it, so the fix recovers the signal the control proved was there and does not yet go past it. Seed spread is 7.9 points, so the mean is the claim and no single seed's number should be quoted.
impact: It closes the rung 0 diagnosis and it indicts the reporting. Four experiments went after context, capacity and corpus size because the total loss fell 90% throughout while the choice head did nothing, and train accuracy -- the one number that separates 'did not generalise' from 'never fitted' -- was not being measured at all. Rung 0's earlier results are NOT evidence that a byte-level System-1 model cannot do this task.
workaround: Three fixes shipped with the finding rather than the number alone. (1) _fit_gate: a ledger metric on whether the choice head beat a constant predictor on its own training rows, kept deliberately separate from _accuracy_gate because the same arithmetic carries opposite verdicts on the two sides. (2) span_weight now enters the recipe_hash, without which the five sweep points hash identically and the ledger records one protocol for runs whose train accuracy differs by 29 points. (3) A non-positive --span-weight is refused from argv rather than inside the seed loop, which on the GH200 is minutes of corpus work spent to reach a verdict that was decidable before any of it.
action_required: CLOSED for rung 0. Two candidates from the parent gap remain untested: mean-pooling an 8192-byte context into 128 dimensions, and lr=3e-3 chosen for a memorisable toy batch. Also untested: whether a lower span_weight costs SPAN accuracy, which sat at 0.7-2.0% against 0.5% chance throughout and was never working to begin with. The same shape on the FT path is opened separately as GAP-FT-PATH-SUMS-TWO-CHANNELS-AND-RECORDS-ONLY-THE-TOTAL.

question: A shard set's header carries data_snapshot_hash, tokenizer_hash and shard_hash. Is that enough to know a run may train on it?
answer: NO. tools/real_ft_run.py does not read labels out of the shard set -- it RECONSTRUCTS them from the repository at --rev through qd_data.mixture and qd_data.render, which are the WORKING TREE's, not the rev's. A change to those modules therefore invalidates an existing shard set, and nothing in the header can see it: the header hashes the corpus, not the code that turns the corpus into rows.
evidence: Measured today. The shard set at /home/ubuntu/shardset (created 2026-09-20T18:06Z, data_snapshot_hash 85acf409..., 341 sequences, 86 span rows) is the one ledger rows 4541d72e / 5ebebda7 / 6374e188 trained on. Against the CURRENT tree the same reconstruction yields 321 labels, and regenerating through tools/real_tokenizer_pipeline.py at the identical --rev and --max-pairs produces a shard set of exactly 321 sequences, 78 span rows, vocab 13787 against 14016, data_snapshot_hash 101168a9... (ledger row 46e63ff3). The box's qd_data and qd_train files are byte-identical to this repository's -- md5 compared on five files -- so the drift is between the SHARD SET and the code, not between hosts.
impact: The safety net held and is the reason this is a gap rather than an incident: real_ft_run refused with 'the reconstructed row order disagrees with supervision.npz: 321 labels against 341 sequences ... Every label would be on the wrong sequence' before any optimizer step. Had it compared only counts, or trusted data_snapshot_hash, it would have trained 321 labels onto 341 sequences. What remains true is that the invalidation is invisible until a training run is attempted, so a shard set can be carried forward for days looking current.
workaround: Regenerate rather than reconcile. /home/ubuntu/shardset-v2 is the current corpus code's shard set and is what subsequent runs use. The stale one is kept, not deleted, because three ledger rows name it.
action_required: OPEN. The header should carry a hash of the generating code -- the qd_data / qd_train modules that produce rows -- alongside data_snapshot_hash, so a stale set is detectable when it is READ rather than when it is trained on. Not implemented here: it touches the shard header format, which several tools parse, and that is a decision about the format rather than a fix to this tool.

question: GAP-RUNG0-THE-UNWEIGHTED-SUM-PINS-THE-CHOICE-HEAD-AT-THE-PRIOR found rung 0's constraint in an unweighted sum of two channels that open 6.2:1 apart. QwenDecisionStep -- the step train_ft drives -- sums the same way and defaults span_weight to 1.0, and no caller in this repository had ever passed one. What is that ratio on the path final training uses?
answer: 39.7:1, measured on the real 1.4B tower. The letter channel opens at 6.9002 and the span channel at 274.1343, summed unweighted, so what the optimiser minimises is very nearly the pointer loss alone. Rung 0's choice head was pinned at its training set's majority share at an EFFECTIVE ratio of roughly 1.2:1 or above; this path sits thirty times past that.
evidence: Ledger rows f5d50f16 (ft) and 419ed2ce (verdict) in ledger/gh200-2026-09-21.jsonl, chain verifying at 227 rows, metric objective_channel_balance_at_open = 39.73. AUDIT/ft-channel-balance-2026-09-21.json. The run itself was 2 passes over 10 batches -- 20 optimizer steps -- and both floor gates correctly FAILED (letter gap 1.157, span gap 67.578, bar 0.05). That is the right reading of a 20-step run. The opening ratio is taken at the first micro-batch and is unaffected by it.
impact: It is a measured risk on the path that matters, and it is NOT a demonstrated failure. Two things argue against panic. The only converged real-tower runs on this path -- 4541d72e / 5ebebda7 / 6374e188 -- drove BOTH channels to their floors (letter 3.36e-06, span 0.000000, verdict row 835d9931), but those were memorisation runs whose floors were both 0.0, which is headroom a real task will not have. And unlike rung 0, this path already fails a per-channel floor gate when a channel is starved, through the single owner _floor_state -- so the failure mode would be loud here rather than silent.
workaround: Three things shipped rather than a changed default. (1) --span-weight now exists on tools/real_ft_run.py and reaches BOTH the real step and the stand-in; it defaults to 1.0, DELIBERATELY unchanged, because rung 0's threshold was measured on a 1.5M byte model and transferring it to a 1.4B backbone would be an inference wearing a gate's clothes. (2) objective_channel_balance_at_open is recorded and explicitly not gated, so the quantity is in the ledger and can be asked of real rows later instead of re-derived from a run that is gone. (3) RealFtStep had NO span_weight at all while QwenDecisionStep had one nobody passed, so the tool's two branches summed their channels by two different rules -- exactly the drift HANDOFF/backbone-2026-09-20.md warned about. They now weight it identically.
action_required: OPEN. The experiment that would settle it is a non-memorisation FT run at a nonzero floor, at span_weight 1.0 against something well below it, reading the per-channel floor gates. That is a real epoch rather than a 20-step probe and belongs with the cost approval rule 4 requires if it grows past a single short single-GPU job.

question: The first version of this record measured the FT objective's opening balance and stopped there. A ratio is not a failure. What does the imbalance actually cost?
answer: It costs the letter channel its floor, and lowering span_weight buys it back. Same plan, same seed, same 128 optimizer steps, both channel floors measured at 0.0 so both are fully fittable: at span_weight 1.0 the letter channel ends 0.0997 above the floor and FAILS its gate (bar 0.05); at 0.05 it ends 0.0055 above and PASSES. An 18x smaller gap. The span channel moves the other way, 0.0514 to 0.1352, which is the trade rather than a surprise -- one gradient budget, spent differently.
evidence: AUDIT/ft-span-weight-paired-2026-09-21.json. Ledger rows e1ec8f57/115f24b4 (1.0) and d7241bfa/4fe1aee7 (0.05) in ledger/gh200-2026-09-21.jsonl, chain verifying at 231 rows. Opening balance 260.44:1 and 7.71:1 respectively -- both from the PRE-FIX reading that took each channel's first nonzero log entry independently rather than one micro-batch carrying both, which is why they are not exactly a 20x pair. Direction and magnitude hold; the exact figures are superseded for later rows.
impact: This is NOT rung 0's collapse, and the difference matters for what to do about it. Rung 0's choice head sat exactly at its training set's majority share and had learned nothing conditional about a single row. Here the letter channel falls from ~2.07 to within 0.0997 of zero at span_weight 1.0 -- a 95% reduction and a model that plainly learned. The FT path DEGRADES under the imbalance where rung 0 STOPPED. Most likely capacity, 1.4B parameters against 1.5M, but this experiment does not isolate the cause.
workaround: The default stays at 1.0 and this does not justify moving it. One seed on a zero-floor memorisation task is not evidence a default deserves -- the rung-0 sweep needed five seeds to separate signal from a 7.9-point spread -- and the span channel's own gate got WORSE at 0.05, so there is a real cost on the other side. The right weight is a measurement nobody has taken, not a smaller number.
action_required: OPEN, and now specific. Three things this did not do: multiple seeds per arm; a corpus with a NONZERO floor, which the 2026-09-20 shard set had through contradictory span twins and the current one does not; and a longer schedule, since 128 steps may simply be short of where the 1.0 arm closes its own gap. A seeded sweep over span_weight on this path is the experiment, and at ~110 s per arm it is minutes of single-GPU time rather than a rule-4 job.

tool: read of Makefile and python/qd_train/ledger.py; make gates
question: Re-verified while auditing what a full train needs: does `make gates` still report PASS without examining the torch-only modules?
answer: NO -- this is CLOSED and the record had gone stale. The Makefile defines TORCH_PYTEST_CMD and a `torch-pytest` target, and LEDGER_RECORD_CMD passes `--suite pytest_torch_python_tests=...` alongside the cargo and repo-venv suites. `gates` runs lint, clippy, ledger-record and ledger-verify; ledger-record is what executes all three suites.

question: Re-verified while auditing what a full train needs: does tools/real_ft_run.py still drive the real 1.4B tower at the stand-in's lr, and still accept --hidden/--heads that it silently ignores?
answer: NO to both -- CLOSED, record stale. STANDIN_LR=3e-3 and REAL_BACKBONE_LR=1e-5 are separate constants (:169, :173), and --lr is a None sentinel resolved per branch (:1873, :1885). --hidden and --heads are REFUSED under --real-backbone (:1859-1871) rather than accepted and ignored, with the reasoning the record asked for: 'accepting them would put a number in the ledger recipe that determined nothing, and recipe feeds recipe_hash'.

question: Auditing what a full train needs: `trainer.py` promises a bit-exact resume and `test_trainer.py` proves it. Does that property hold for the step a full train actually runs?
answer: NO. Every resume test in this repository drove `TinyStep`, a test double. `QwenDecisionStep.state()` returned the tower's weights, the span head's weights, `micro_batches`, `span_weight` and `vocab_size` -- and NOT the optimizer. A resume therefore restored the parameters exactly and reset AdamW's `exp_avg`, `exp_avg_sq` and step count to zero, re-entering warm-up on a trained model.
evidence: Measured on a tiny real Qwen3_5TextModel through the real loop: 12 FT steps taken as one run, against the same 12 taken as 6+6 across a checkpoint written to and read from a real file. 5 of the 12 losses differ -- step 7 gives 3.431338 against the uninterrupted 3.440382 -- and every divergence is in the post-resume leg. The weights restore bit-exactly; only what the next step does with them differs, which is why nothing had caught it.
impact: This was the blocker for a full train. A rented GH200 interrupted at hour three would have come back to a model with the right weights and an optimizer that forgot everything, and the loss curve would have looked unremarkable across the seam. It also silently discards the point of the fp32-master recipe: MasterWeightAdamW's masters were not in the checkpoint either, so a resume would have rebuilt them from the bf16 parameters -- exactly the rounded copy the class exists to avoid.
workaround: FIXED. `state()` carries `optimizer` and `load_state()` requires it -- by name, because a weights-only state loaded without complaint and resumed a run whose moments were zero, which looks like a working resume. The serialiser walks the `state_dict` generically, so it handles both `torch.optim.AdamW`'s {state, param_groups} and MasterWeightAdamW's {inner, masters} without naming either; the one structural fact encoded is that `state` is keyed by parameter INDEX, which the checkpoint body must stringify and the reload must restore. The optimizer is loaded AFTER the parameters, because `torch.optim.Optimizer.load_state_dict` casts each restored tensor to the dtype and device of the parameter it belongs to.
action_required: The step now resumes. What still has no owner is the DRIVER: HANDOFF/resume-2026-09-20.md recorded that no tool in tools/ passes `on_checkpoint`, and that is still true -- `Checkpoint.write` is called only from tests. tools/real_ft_run.py is explicit that it never resumes (RealFtStep.load_state raises). A full train needs a driver that passes the hooks; the machinery under it is now proven on the real step rather than on a double.

question: HANDOFF/resume-2026-09-20.md: 'No caller passed the hooks. Checkpoint.write and Checkpoint.read are called in exactly two files, both of them test files. No driver in tools/ writes a checkpoint, so nothing on disk survives a kill ... which is still nobody's job. That last piece is the first command for the next lane.' Is it somebody's job yet?
answer: YES. tools/real_ft_run.py sets RunControl.checkpoint_every and passes on_checkpoint and resume_from. Proven on the REAL 1.4B tower rather than a tiny one: the run wrote checkpoints at steps 20, 40 and 60; the process was SIGKILLed with no cleanup and reported no result; a second invocation with --resume-from printed 'at optimizer step 60, batch index 60, seed 0', continued through 80 and 100, and terminated steps_exhausted at the full 128.
evidence: Ledger rows 23c8ff9a (ft) and efabded9 (verdict) in ledger/gh200-2026-09-21.jsonl, chain verifying at 253 rows, train.optimizer_steps=128, train.termination=steps_exhausted. The resumed run opened with a letter loss of 0.0034 against ~2.0 on a fresh one, which is what coming back trained looks like. Each checkpoint is 7.93 GiB written in ~10.4 s.
impact: A rented box interrupted mid-run is now recoverable on cuda, which is the property the whole S5 resume design existed for and which nothing had ever exercised outside a test double. Note the operational consequence the write timing exposes: at ~1.5 s/step a 20-step interval spends a third of its wall clock writing, so a full train wants a far larger interval. The driver now prints the size and duration beside the step so that interval is chosen from a measurement.
workaround: Two refusals are the load-bearing part. Checkpointing is refused on the STAND-IN branch, because RealFtStep.load_state raises by design and a file written from it would look like a resume point and never be one. And --resume-from is routed against the plan at argv time: a checkpoint from a device --devices does not list, a seed --seeds does not list, or an 'epoch' checkpoint without --epoch are all refused before a 24-second tower load.
action_required: RESOLVED for the happy path. Still open: a DRIVER-level test that a resume onto a different corpus order is refused. trainer.py rehashes the consumed prefix and test_trainer.py covers it with TinyStep only; the end-to-end run above exercises the case where the order is right.

question: The record's action_required: the header should carry a hash of the generating code -- the qd_data modules that produce rows -- so a stale set is detectable when it is READ rather than when it is trained on.
answer: IMPLEMENTED. ShardHeader carries code_fingerprint: {module name: sha256} over every *.py in qd_data, written by write_shards from the modules LOADED in the writing process. assert_shard_trainable -- the trainer's door -- reports shard_code_current and raises ShardContractViolation on a mismatch unless allow_stale_code=True. ShardReader calls that door in its constructor, so the answer arrives at open() rather than at the first optimizer step.
evidence: 10 tests fail against the pre-fix consumers and pass after: 8 in python/tests/test_fingerprint.py and 2 end-to-end in python/tests/test_shards.py that write a real shard set and re-open it. Measured by reverting qd_train/artifacts.py and qd_train/shards.py to HEAD in a scratch copy while keeping qd_data/fingerprint.py, so the failures measure the guard and not the newness of the module. Full suites after: 1638 passed / 2 skipped (torch venv), 1413 passed / 20 skipped (repo venv), cargo 362 passed / 0 failed across 23 binaries, ruff clean over python/ and tools/. No Rust parses the shard header, checked: rg over crates/ for data_snapshot_hash|shard_hash|header.json|ShardHeader returns nothing.
impact: The incident this gap records was caught only because the drift also moved the row COUNT -- 321 labels against 341 sequences -- which tools/real_ft_run.py detects by matching the reconstructed order against supervision.npz entry for entry. A change that moves which label attaches to which row WITHOUT moving how many rows there are produced no refusal anywhere. data_snapshot_hash hashes the corpus and nothing hashed the code that turns the corpus into rows; those are two different things that were wearing one guarantee.
workaround: None needed. Sets written before this field carry no fingerprint and are reported NotRun rather than passed -- rule 5's shape at this boundary -- and are still readable, so the three ledger rows naming the stale set keep their evidence. An empty fingerprint contributes nothing to shard_hash, so headers written before the field still verify.
action_required: None for this gap. Two notes for whoever runs the full train: (1) existing shard sets, including ~/shardset-v2 on the GH200, predate the field and will report shard_code_current=NotRun until regenerated -- regenerating is what turns the check on for that set; (2) the fingerprint is over SOURCE BYTES, so a docstring-only edit to any qd_data module invalidates a set. That direction is deliberate -- the refusal names the changed modules -- but it means qd_data edits and shard regeneration are now coupled.

question: ShardHeader now pins the corpus (data_snapshot_hash), the tokenizer, the remap and the generating code (code_fingerprint). Is that everything that determines which rows a shard set contains?
answer: NO. tools/real_tokenizer_pipeline.py takes --rev, 'the revision the corpus is read at', and its own help says why it matters: 'Several lanes commit to this worktree while a run is in progress, so two runs against HEAD hours apart read different corpora.' The rev is not written into the header. data_snapshot_hash is computed over the manifests the run produced, so it moves when the corpus moves -- it identifies the corpus but does not say which revision it was drawn from, and nothing lets a reader ask 'was this built at the rev I think it was'.
evidence: Found while regenerating shardset-v3 on the GH200 to close GAP-SHARD-SET-GOES-STALE-AGAINST-THE-CORPUS-CODE-THAT-REPRODUCES-ITS-LABELS. The rev for the regeneration (0632f693d3b765b726499e7b4bf19c67959b75cb) had to be recovered from the NOTES of ledger row 46e63ff3, not from shardset-v2's header, which does not carry it. A ledger row is the wrong place for it: the header is what a reader has, and a shard set can outlive the row that recorded it or be copied to another host without it -- which is exactly what happened here, since the box's ledger/runs.jsonl and this repository's are different files.
impact: Lower than the code-fingerprint gap and the same shape. A set regenerated at the WRONG rev produces a different corpus that still looks entirely current: its data_snapshot_hash matches itself, its code_fingerprint matches the loaded code, and every check passes. The counts happened to match here (321 sequences, 78 span rows, vocab 13787 for both v2 and v3), which is evidence the rev was right, but counts matching is the accident that made the previous gap visible, not a check.
workaround: Pass --rev explicitly and record it in the invocation; the ledger row's notes carry it. shardset-v3 was built at 0632f693d3b765b726499e7b4bf19c67959b75cb, ledger row a4429c5a-5b87-4cfb-b88b-b1825d54f0e0 in ledger/shardset-v3-2026-09-21.jsonl on the GH200.
action_required: OPEN. ShardHeader should carry the corpus rev alongside code_fingerprint, written by write_shards from what the pipeline was given rather than from HEAD -- the point is what was READ, not where the worktree happens to be. Deferred rather than done here: write_shards does not currently receive the rev (the pipeline resolves it before calling), so this is a signature change through real_tokenizer_pipeline.py, and that tool is another lane's this session.

question: A shard header pins the corpus (data_snapshot_hash), the tokenizer, the remap and since d13cfae the code that turned the corpus into rows (code_fingerprint). None of them covers WHICH REVISION was read. Is a set built from the wrong revision distinguishable from a correct one?
answer: It was NOT. A set built at the wrong rev has a self-consistent data_snapshot_hash (the rows really are the hash of those rows), a matching code_fingerprint (the code really is the code that ran) and passes every check. Recovering the rev required reading the free-text NOTES of ledger row 46e63ff3, which is not a pin. ShardHeader.corpus_rev now records it, shard_hash covers it so it cannot be edited out, and _shard_rev_check is TRI-STATE: NotRun when the header carries none (every set written before today), NotRun when the CALLER named no revision to check against, Ran(passed=False) and a refusal when the two disagree.
evidence: 16 tests, each verified to fail against the pre-fix tree: 6 in test_artifacts.py (header-side, including that an absent rev hashes to what it hashed to before the field existed, so no set on disk is invalidated), 5 in test_shards.py (reader-side, including that allow_rev_mismatch admits the set and still records Ran(passed=False)), 5 in test_repo_git.py (resolve_rev, including two that read the tools' source). make gates RESULT: PASS at 362 cargo, 1431 repo-venv pytest, 1656 torch-venv pytest, chain verifying at 176 rows.
impact: tools/real_ft_run.py does not read labels out of the shard set: it RECONSTRUCTS them from the repository at --rev and pairs them with the set's sequences. The 2026-09-21 mismatch was caught only because the drift happened to move the row COUNT, 321 against 341. A revision that changes which rows exist without changing how many would have paired every label with the wrong sequence and produced no other symptom. That tool now resolves --rev once and passes it as expect_rev, so the answer arrives at open() rather than at the first optimizer step.
workaround: A second defect was found while wiring it and is the reason tools/repo_git.py gained resolve_rev: real_tokenizer_pipeline.py takes --rev with a DEFAULT OF 'HEAD' and resolves it internally into `resolved`, which is what every corpus read uses. Pinning the unresolved argument would have recorded the string 'HEAD' in the header -- worse than recording nothing, because an absent rev reads NotRun while 'HEAD' compares equal to 'HEAD' and reads as VERIFIED. One name, two quantities. Both tools now resolve through one owner, and two tests read their source to keep it that way.
action_required: RESOLVED. Operationally: every shard set that exists today predates the field, including ~/shardset-v2 and ~/shardset-v3 on the GH200, so shard_rev_matches reads NotRun in every row naming them. They are not refused and stay readable. Regenerate before the full train, not after, or the run's own row records 'nobody could tell' on exactly the question the field exists to answer.

tool: tools/real_ft_run.py --seeds 0 0 1 1 on the GH200, then python/qd_train/backbone.py
question: Six runs of one configuration -- same shard set, same 16-batch plan, same 128-step budget, same span_weight, seeds 0 and 1 -- opened at total losses of 253.48, 279.09, 298.44, 334.62, 382.58 and 489.91. Two runs at the SAME seed differed at step one. What does the `seed` in a ledger row determine?
answer: On the real backbone: the batch order, and nothing about the parameters. QwenDecisionStep builds a randomly-initialised SpanPointerHead and python/qd_train/backbone.py contained no torch.manual_seed, no torch.Generator and no seed argument at all. tools/real_ft_run.py's OTHER branch, the stand-in RealFtStep, calls torch.manual_seed(seed) on the first line of __init__ -- so the tool was reproducible on the backbone nobody measures and not on the one every GH200 row used. One name, two behaviours, split across the two branches of one tool. QwenDecisionStep now takes `seed` as a REQUIRED keyword and seeds before it draws anything, matching the stand-in's spelling.
evidence: Ledger rows 2544935f, 70217ccc, 403e43f2, 34ece810 (ft) with verdict rows d79373f4, 1bd7d897, 8aec8a30, e23c81d0 in ledger/gh200-determinism-2026-09-21.jsonl -- one invocation, --seeds 0 0 1 1, four runs. Seed 0 gave final span losses of 0.000000 and 0.086095 and one of the two failed the letter floor gate while the other passed. Plus rows 9441429c/7e24bb57 and 763a9427/b18721f9 in ledger/gh200-smoke-2026-09-21.jsonl, both seed 0, opening at 382.58 and 489.91. Five tests in python/tests/test_backbone.py, each verified to fail against the unseeded class.
impact: The letter channel's head is pretrained and the span channel's is random, so the unseeded draw fell almost entirely on the span channel: across those six runs the final letter loss stayed inside 1.07e-4..8.81e-4 while the final span loss ranged 0.000000..1.823686. That is the shape AUDIT/ft-span-weight-seeded-2026-09-21.json reported as 'the span channel does NOT show a clean opposite trend ... three seeds cannot separate that from noise'. The spread was not seed noise: the seeds were not controlling the quantity that moved. That audit's span-channel column, and the letter-gate-failure counts read per seed, describe a mixture of seed and an unseeded initialisation and cannot be read per seed.
workaround: None was available. The fix is in the class rather than in the driver on purpose: a driver that seeds before each construction gives the same guarantee only until the next caller forgets, or until anything between the seeding and the construction draws a number. test_the_seed_survives_an_arbitrarily_advanced_global_rng advances the ambient stream by a different amount before each build and requires the two steps to still agree.
action_required: RESOLVED for the initialisation. STILL OPEN and separately measurable: how much run-to-run spread remains once the seed is honoured. CUDA kernels with atomics are not bit-reproducible, so 'seeded' is not the same as 'identical', and a number that cannot be reproduced from its own recorded protocol is weaker evidence than it reads as. The overnight run measures the residual before it measures anything else.

question: Which other agents are editing the files this lane touches?
answer: ANSWERED, by a mechanism no lane had tried rather than by a change to GitPulse. `ListAgents` enumerates live sessions on this machine, including peers in the SAME worktree, which is the half gitpulse_insights' collisions facet cannot see because it compares worktrees. `SendMessage` then negotiates file ownership between them. That is the missing facet the records asked for, and it is available to every agent here. CLAUDE.md's navigation section carried the defect too -- it claimed gitpulse_insights 'names ... live agent sessions' -- and now states the worktree/same-worktree split and names ListAgents as step 3.
evidence: Measured 2026-09-21 in this worktree. ListAgents returned 'Qwen decision system audit and hardening [144c37] - interactive - busy', a peer session editing the same files; SendMessage then split the tree by file (it took tools/real_ft_run.py, python/tests/test_real_ft_protocol.py, qd_train/backbone.py, qd_train/optim.py, ledger/*, AUDIT/*; this lane took python/qd_data/ and its tests) and both lanes committed without a clobber -- 3f06c41, 47fbbba, d13cfae, 96f6de4, d920bc7 interleaved cleanly. The same session's GitPulse brief reported 2 worktrees and named gaps.jsonl contended BETWEEN worktrees, and said nothing about the peer inside this one, which is exactly the blind spot these records describe.
impact: This record previously told the next agent it was blind, which invites the uncoordinated write it warned about. An agent that reads overlapping_files=0 as safety will clobber work in flight; an agent that runs ListAgents will not.
workaround: None needed. ListAgents, then SendMessage, before touching a file.
action_required: None. CLAUDE.md now carries it as navigation step 3 so every lane prompt gets it. Two habits go with it, both learned the same day: never `git stash` or `git add -A` in a shared worktree, and append to gaps.jsonl with O_APPEND + fsync rather than read-modify-write.

question: The record: whoever wires on_checkpoint must choose between one slot rewritten in place and a step-N series, and say which. Has that choice been made?
answer: YES -- ONE SLOT, rewritten in place, chosen when on_checkpoint was wired in 3f06c41. tools/real_ft_run.py:1484 writes to `checkpoint_dir / _checkpoint_name(tag, seed, device)`, one file per cell of the (tag x seed x device) product, and Checkpoint.write is atomic -- temp file in the target's directory, fsync, rename, fsync the directory -- so the previous checkpoint stays readable until the instant the new one replaces it.
evidence: The reasoning is recorded at the write site: 'Keeping a series would be a retention policy, and this is a resume point rather than a history.' The record's own constraint is honoured -- no deletion policy was put inside Checkpoint.write, which is the module that must never lose a checkpoint.
impact: The choice was load-bearing for disk on the GH200: this model's checkpoint is ~8.5 GB (weights plus both AdamW moments), so a step-N series over a full train would have filled the box.
workaround: None needed.
action_required: None. The per-cell filename was a separate defect found and fixed the same day: without the device in the name, cpu and mps at one seed collide, and the trainer cannot catch it because both share a seed AND a schedule.

tool: python/tests? none -- gaps.jsonl is parsed by no code in this repository
question: How many gaps are open? Asked while trying to close all of them, which requires knowing which ones are open.
answer: THE COUNT IS AMBIGUOUS AND EVERY NAIVE ANSWER IS WRONG. Taking the last record per id, the status field holds five distinct values: open (90), resolved (72), closed (64), resolved-with-residual (22), closed-no-defect (6). A reader that treats {resolved, closed} as closed counts 118 open; a reader that also counts resolved-with-residual and closed-no-defect as closed counts 90. The 28 difference are records that ARE closed and read as open.
evidence: Measured 2026-09-21 over 405 records / 254 distinct ids. This session's own first pass reported 118 open and had to be corrected to 90 -- which is the defect doing its work on the agent trying to fix it.
impact: This is the repository's own recurring defect class, one name and two quantities, in the file that records that defect class. Nothing in the repository parses gaps.jsonl -- it is read by humans and agents only -- so the ambiguity has never failed a gate, which is exactly why it survived. Any report that states a gap count without saying which convention it used is unfalsifiable.
workaround: Treat {resolved, closed, resolved-with-residual, closed-no-defect} as closed and {open} as open, and say so when quoting a count. resolved-with-residual means the record's question is answered and a NAMED narrower thing remains, which is normally recorded as its own gap.
action_required: OPEN. Either pin the vocabulary to a fixed set with a checker that runs in `make gates` -- gaps.jsonl is currently validated by nothing, so a typo'd status is silently a new category -- or collapse the five values to {open, closed} with the residual carried as a separate record. Not done here: it is a format decision over a file two lanes are appending to concurrently, and it wants the human who reads these counts to pick.

question: Commit fad5315's message says: 'One transient failure of test_the_repositorys_own_ledgers_are_checked_not_assumed was observed and did not reproduce -- the other lane was mid-write on a new ledger file when the suite read it.' Was it transient?
answer: NO. The failure was deterministic and had a cause. The test asserts len(find_forks(ledger/*.jsonl)) == 1; a new ledger file, ledger/gh200-overnight-2026-09-21.jsonl, starts its own chain at genesis, so find_forks reports a second group -- a ROOT fork (gh200-2026-09-20.jsonl:1 against gh200-overnight-2026-09-21.jsonl:1, prev_row_hash=None). It reproduced for the lane that caused it. My re-run passed only because that lane had already changed the test.
evidence: Reported by the concurrent lane, which diagnosed and fixed it. The underlying conflation is the interesting part and is theirs: find_forks distinguishes a DIVERGENCE (two rows claiming one shared predecessor -- a copied ledger both sides appended to, which is what the detector is for) from a ROOT fork (two unrelated files), and the test counted both. So a per-host ledger -- the fix named in GAP-LEDGER-NO-STORY-FOR-A-CHAIN-FORKED-ACROSS-TWO-MACHINES -- registered as the disease. The test now counts divergences and allows at most one root group.
impact: Two failures of mine, and the second is the one that matters. (1) I ran the test once, saw it pass, and concluded 'did not reproduce' from a single re-run -- the repository's own rule is that a failing case which passes on the first re-run means the diagnosis is wrong, and I read it as meaning the failure was not real. (2) I invented a mechanism -- a mid-write race -- that fit the symptom and checked none of it, then put it in a commit message, where it is unamendable once commits land on top. A plausible story that fits the evidence is not the cause, and a commit message is the worst place to put one.
workaround: Read the message of fad5315 with this record beside it. The claim is wrong; the rest of that commit stands.
action_required: None mechanical. The habit: attribute a failure only after reproducing it or reading the assertion, and never put an unverified cause in a commit message, which cannot be corrected in place the way a file can.

The choice head is pinned at the class prior there regardless of what any other lever does, so a sweep run at that point cannot show a lever helping and its null result is not evidence about the lever. This record's own evidence is the collapse signature rather than a capacity ceiling: 'all three seeds scored 0.5215 to four decimals -- 158 of 303 rows, the exact size of the stub class -- so each model answers stub on every held-out row.' A 23.8M-parameter model answering one class on every row is not a model that ran out of capacity.

Three sizes x three seeds, ~111-790s per seed on the GH200. question: Rule 8 makes three seeds the floor for a run that may inform a decision. For rung 0's measured seed-to-seed spread, what effect size does three seeds actually resolve?
answer: ~7.4 PERCENTAGE POINTS, which is larger than the entire signal in the corpus. From the span-weight sweep's own five seeds at span_weight=0.05 -- val accuracies 0.587, 0.545, 0.571, 0.617, 0.538 -- the standard deviation is 0.0322. Comparing two points at n=3 gives SE(difference) = 0.0263, so a ~2.8 SE difference is 7.4pp. The linear control beats the majority baseline by 5.3pp, and that is the whole of the extractable signal anyone has demonstrated. A three-seed sweep therefore cannot distinguish 'this lever does nothing' from 'this lever doubles the only signal we have'.
evidence: n=3 resolves 7.4pp, n=5 resolves 5.7pp, n=8 resolves 4.5pp, at 2.8 SE on a two-point comparison with sd=0.0322. The effect being chased is 5.3pp, which is 1.56 sd -- signal and seed noise are the same size. The capacity sweep (AUDIT/rung0-capacity-sweep-2026-09-20.json) used three seeds and reported differences of -1.4pp, 0.0pp, -1.2pp and -0.3pp as evidence of no effect; every one of those is far inside the noise floor of its own design.
impact: Independent of, and additional to, GAP-RUNG0-SWEEPS-BEFORE-THE-SPAN-WEIGHT-FLAG-MEASURED-A-PINNED-HEAD. Even had the capacity sweep run at a working span_weight, three seeds could not have detected the effect it was looking for. Two independent reasons its null is uninformative. More generally: rule 8's three-seed floor is a floor on ADMISSIBILITY and is being read as sufficiency. A null result from a three-seed sweep on this corpus means 'no effect larger than about 7pp' and is routinely written down as 'no effect'.
workaround: State the resolvable effect size beside every null. The capacity re-run at span_weight=0.05 uses five seeds and pre-registers its floor at ~5.7pp, so a null there will be reported as 'no effect larger than 5.7pp' rather than as 'no effect'.
action_required: OPEN, and it is a gate question, so rule 2 puts it out of an agent's reach: this reports that three seeds is under-powered for this corpus's noise, and does not move the threshold. For a human: either raise the seed floor for rung 0 measurements specifically, or require that a reported null carry the effect size its design could have detected. The second is cheaper and generalises -- it is the same discipline as 'never present a capped sample as complete coverage', applied to statistical power rather than to sampling.

question: GAP-FT-128-STEP-SPREAD-IS-AN-UNCONVERGED-BUDGET concluded from phase 4 that most of the 128-step run-to-run spread was an unconverged budget rather than nondeterministic kernels. That was an inference, not a measurement. Which is it?
answer: THE KERNELS. Eight repeats of the identical configuration with torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) came back BIT-IDENTICAL -- total 518.5886 -> 0.000078, letter 1.9029 -> 0.000078, span 518.5886 -> 0.000000, every run, every digit. Without it the same eight gave final span losses of 0.000000 .. 1.505752 with 3 of 8 over the bar. The run also completed rather than raising, which establishes that every op this model uses has a deterministic implementation.
evidence: ledger/gh200-det-2026-09-21.jsonl, ft rows 7da24558, 7ea977cd, 67f4dc76, d5a04578, b15c3b63, 3c5fc10f, 9a39f9b7, 281e854b. Compare AUDIT/ft-overnight-2026-09-21.json arm p1-residual-seed0-x8 for the same configuration without the flag. Price measured over the same eight: 131.3 s per run against 111.4 s, 18% wall clock.
impact: The corrected reading, which needs both measurements: kernel nondeterminism is the SOURCE, and non-convergence is the AMPLIFIER -- at 512 steps the spread collapses to [0.00000, 0.00012] WITHOUT determinism, because a converged run stops amplifying the perturbation. Removing either removes the symptom, which is why inferring the cause from the 512-step arms alone was wrong. A long schedule hides this rather than fixing it.
workaround: The superseded record's conclusions about span_weight are UNAFFECTED and stand: at 512 steps both arms reach both floors on 5 of 5 seeds, at 128 the arms are not separable from the residual, and the default stays at 1.0. What changes is the attribution of the residual, and with it the recommendation: a full train should pass --deterministic, at 18% wall clock, which is the opposite of what that record and the flag's own help string said.
action_required: RESOLVED. The correction is recorded in three places besides this one -- the flag's help, the deterministic_kernels NotRun reason, and AUDIT/ft-overnight-2026-09-21.json under correction_the_residual_is_the_kernels -- because all three carried the reversed claim.

question: The FT path was assumed reproducible at a fixed seed for three days and was not (GAP-FT-RUNS-ARE-NOT-REPRODUCIBLE-AT-A-FIXED-SEED). Is rung 0?
answer: NO, it was not, and now it can be. With --deterministic, added in a401939, two repeats are BIT-IDENTICAL on every printed figure: total 2.5863 -> 0.5486, choice 1.921 -> 0.538, val 53.8%, train 64.6%, span start 0.7% end 1.4%; only wall clock differs, 239.0s against 239.1s.

question: The power analysis both lanes are now sizing experiments from takes sd = 0.0322 from five seeds of the rung-0 span-weight sweep at 0.05 (0.587, 0.545, 0.571, 0.617, 0.538) and derives a minimum resolvable difference of ~7.4 pp at n=3, ~5.7 pp at n=5. Is 0.0322 seed variation?
answer: NO. It is seed variation PLUS kernel nondeterminism, and the two are not separated by anything anyone has run. The concurrent lane measured rung 0 at a fixed seed: two runs, same corpus by sha256, same 727/288 decisions, same 49.0% baseline, gave choice val 50.3% and 53.1%. 2.8 pp apart at one seed, on a corpus whose entire demonstrated signal is 5.3 pp. So 0.0322 is an UPPER BOUND on the seed-only sd, and the true value is unmeasured.
evidence: sd recomputed here from the five published values: 0.0322, matching. Minimum resolvable difference at alpha=.05 two-sided, power .80: 7.4 pp at n=3, 5.7 at n=5, 4.5 at n=8, 3.7 at n=12. The fixed-seed pair is the concurrent lane's, reported before it launched anything, and is what a401939 (--deterministic on tools/rung0_real_run.py) was written in response to; two deterministic repeats are bit-identical on every printed figure.
impact: Which way it cuts depends on the design, and both directions matter. For a sweep run as all of them were -- nondeterministic -- 0.0322 IS the right statistic and the 7.4 pp floor is correct, so the criticism of the capacity and context sweeps stands exactly as written. For a DETERMINISTIC sweep the relevant sd is seed-only and smaller, so the floor improves by an unknown amount: a crude estimate from the single pair puts sd_seed in 0.020-0.029 depending on the correction factor used for n=2, and one pair is a poor variance estimator whichever is chosen.
workaround: Determinism buys statistical power as well as reproducibility, and not for free. At rung 0's MEASURED 2.3x cost (239.0s against 103.0s -- NOT the FT path's 18%, which does not transfer) spending the same GPU-hours on more nondeterministic seeds is roughly break-even on resolution, and which side of break-even it lands on turns on exactly the sd the single pair cannot pin down.
action_required: OPEN, and cheap to close: five deterministic seeds at one configuration measures the seed-only sd directly. The concurrent lane's phase 0 is that run and is in flight. Until it lands, no sweep should be SIZED from 0.0322 -- reporting a null against it remains correct for a nondeterministic design.

tool: a survey of ledger/*.jsonl, 799 rows across 5 chain files
question: Rule 4 requires every 8xH100 job to carry a cost estimate, and RunRecorder has a cost_usd field for it. What is in that field?
answer: 0.0, on all 799 rows, without exception -- the set of distinct values over every ledger in this repository is exactly {0.0}. RunRecorder's cost_usd_per_hour defaults to 0.0 and no caller has ever passed one, so cost_usd is the product of a rate nobody set and a duration that is itself wrong on 43% of rows (GAP-RUNCORDER-WALL-CLOCK-MEASURES-THE-ROW-WRITE, the concurrent lane's).
evidence: Surveyed independently of the lane that raised the wall-clock half: 799 rows, 346 under 0.1s wall clock (43%), and cost_usd distinct values {0.0: 799}. The GH200 has been rented and running since 2026-09-20; not one row prices it.
impact: A field that is always zero records nothing while reading as a measurement, which is the same defect as transformers_sha='unknown' and as a seed that named the batch order. It matters more than those because rule 4 makes a cost estimate a PRECONDITION for launching an 8xH100 job: the mechanism by which that rule is satisfied currently produces 0.0 whatever the job costs, so a human approving a run on the strength of a recorded estimate would be approving on the strength of a default.
workaround: None. Reading a cost out of any existing row gives 0.0 and the ledger is append-only, so no past row can be corrected. Until this closes, rule 4's cost estimate has to be stated by a human in the request, not read from the ledger.
action_required: OPEN. The fix lives in python/qd_train/ledger.py, which the concurrent lane holds for the wall-clock change; the two are coupled, because a correct cost needs a correct duration first. Sequencing suggestion, not a claim: wall clock first, then a required rather than defaulted cost_usd_per_hour on the same argument -- a rate nobody set and a rate of zero must not be one number.

question: rung 0 ledger rows record wall_clock_s 7.379e-05 and cost_usd 0.0 for runs the same process printed at 239.0s. Is that one bad row, one bad tool, or the recorder?
answer: The recorder, and it is 43% of the ledger. RunRecorder._finish computed wall = time.monotonic() - self._t0 with _t0 set in __enter__, so a caller that does the work FIRST and enters the recorder to report it records how long it took to write the row. 346 of 799 rows carry wall_clock_s under 0.1s. cost_usd = cost_usd_per_hour * wall / 3600 is derived from the same number, so those rows price a GPU hour at zero.
evidence: Survey over ledger/*.jsonl, 799 rows, reproduced independently by the audit lane. By tool, rows under 0.1s: rung0_real_run.py 53 of 53; rung0_toy_run.py 36 of 36; real_tokenizer_pipeline 22 of 22; rung0_linear_control.py 1 of 1; real_ft_run.py 162 of 348, which is exactly its 162 smoke rows against 186 ft rows at min 21.7s / median 117.5s / max 1737.1s; ft_toy_run.py 72 of 156, exactly its 72 smoke rows; build rows 0 of 139, because record_build wraps its suites in the with-block. Fixed in a409895.
impact: Three things. (1) No rung 0 or smoke row in this repository predating a409895 records how long its run took; the number there is the time to write the row. (2) LedgerRow validated durations with `wall_clock_s < 0`, and `nan < 0` is False, so a NaN duration and a NaN cost could reach the ledger and every mean computed over it. (3) The two tools that get ft right get smoke wrong, so the defect was invisible to anyone checking a single file: the same tool produced correct and incorrect rows side by side.
workaround: wall_clock_s is now a required keyword on RunRecorder with no default. None means the with-block contains the run and should be timed; a number means the caller measured the run. Required rather than defaulted because a default reproducing the old behaviour is the same bug under a new name. LedgerRow now rejects non-finite durations and costs via math.isfinite.
action_required: None for the mechanism. Rows already written are not retro-fixable and should not be read for duration or cost: the value recorded is real, it is just not the run's. See GAP-COST-USD-IS-ZERO-ON-EVERY-ROW-EVER-WRITTEN for the half this does not close -- cost_usd_per_hour still defaults to 0.0, so cost is 0 on every row even where the duration is now right.

question: Before making wall_clock_s a required argument: what constructs RunRecorder? A required argument breaks every call site, so the list has to be complete.
answer: DevMap could not answer it completely. The call returned 10 callers and set walk_incomplete on BOTH directions: 'stopped at depth 3; the result is a lower bound, not the full blast radius; 16950 of 36550 unresolved attribution sites have no indexed target'. A lower bound is not an enumeration, and the answer also exceeded the token budget and had to be read back from the spill file.
evidence: walk_incomplete present on neighbors.0.callers and neighbors.0.callees; hidden=0 on both, so the truncation is in the walk rather than the rendering. Second signal used instead: rg for 'RunRecorder(' across tools/ and python/, plus rg for bare 'RunRecorder' to catch aliasing or indirect construction, which found none -- every non-call reference is an import, a type annotation or a docstring. Third signal: running the suites, which found 52 failures across 5 files. The test run is the only one of the three that is an enumeration rather than a search, and it is what the final count rests on.

Both lanes' first estimates were wrong from search alone -- 21 and 'about 30' against an actual 52 -- which is the point: neither the graph nor grep was the thing that knew.

question: The capacity sweep at span_weight 0.05 ran 128x2 to completion over 8 seeds and then failed both larger points immediately. Why, and is the comparison still available?
answer: CUDA OOM at the default --batch-size 16, inside the pre-training evaluate(), before a single optimizer step. 256x4/h8 at 8192 bytes asked for 25.71 GiB on top of 89.86 GiB already held by the process, against 94.50 GiB total. 512x6 failed the same way. Not a leak and not a missing no_grad -- evaluate() already uses torch.no_grad() and model.eval() (rung0_real_run.py:375,382). It is the attention matrix: 16 rows x 8 heads x 8192^2 x 4 bytes is 34 GiB for one layer's scores, and torch._transformer_encoder_layer_fwd materialises it.
evidence: Traceback at rung0_real_run.py:556 -> :386 -> byte_decider.py:170 -> torch/nn/modules/transformer.py:921. The 128x2 point completed 8 of 8 seeds at the same batch size, 460 steps, 102.9-103.0s each. The script reported both failures as 'point NOT measured' and continued rather than passing them off as results: 'PHASE1 INCOMPLETE -- not measured: 256x4:rc1 512x6:rc1'.
impact: The capacity question is unanswered, for the third time and for a third distinct reason: first the span_weight confound, then n=3 against a 5.3pp signal, now an OOM. The 128x2 arm IS measured and is not affected. The fix is not free: batch_size is inside recipe_hash, correctly, so lowering it for the two large points makes them a different protocol from the 128x2 arm already run, and that arm has to be re-run at the same batch size or the three points are not a comparison.
workaround: Probe the largest batch size 512x6 actually fits (1 seed, 1 epoch), then run all THREE points at it. Do not lower the batch only for the points that need it.
action_required: Open. Also worth knowing before reading the 2026-09-20 sweep: that sweep ran the same three points at the same 8192 bytes and the same batch size on the same box and same torch (2.10.0+cu128) WITHOUT OOM, on a corpus at rev 261c538 with 763 train decisions against this one's 727. Similar decision counts, different context-length distributions, so the batches bucket differently. That difference has not been measured and is the reason a batch size that worked once is not evidence it works now.

question: Every GPU row this project has written records code_commit '8b9df39bf816d149efc108e3581ab4ba8192688f-dirty'. What does that pin?
answer: Less than it looks. The box's checkout is at 8b9df39 with 72 modified or untracked paths and 6894 insertions across 29 tracked files. In this instance the answer was recoverable by hashing files individually, and it is good: tools/rung0_real_run.py on the box is byte-identical to the local commit dec1bce, which was HEAD when the sweep launched, and python/qd_train/byte_decider.py is byte-identical to the local tree. So the sweep ran the code it was supposed to -- but the ledger row does not say so, and nothing would have caught it if it had not.
evidence: sha256 of tools/rung0_real_run.py: box e1f89d9e7352ee49cb87, local dec1bce e1f89d9e7352ee49cb87, local a401939 e1f89d9e7352ee49cb87, local a409895 099ec512cbc4d7f703c2 (differs only by the wall_clock_s fix landed after the sweep launched). byte_decider.py 939d20067fa0c9fe4464 on both sides. A row whose code provenance is 'some commit, plus 6894 lines of something' supports the citation only as far as someone is willing to hash files by hand afterwards. The same function pointed at qd_train plus the invoking tool would make a run's code provenance a map of hashes instead of a dirty bit. Not done here because it is a ledger row-schema change and the schema was already being changed for wall_clock_s.

question: The capacity sweep holds --span-weight at 0.05 and varies width/layers/heads, so that capacity is the only thing that moves. Does a fixed span_weight actually hold the objective fixed?
answer: NO, and the difference grows with capacity. The two channels do not open at the same place at different sizes. Measured at initialisation on the same corpus, same split, same 8192-byte context: at 128x2/h4 span opens at 13.312 against choice 1.921, a 6.9:1 ratio; at 512x6/h8 span opens at 31.982 against choice 3.409, a 9.4:1 ratio. Both are above ln(8192)=9.01, so the span head starts worse than a uniform pointer and more so at the larger width -- a logit-scale-at-initialisation effect. A single scalar span_weight therefore lands on a different effective objective at each point of the sweep.
evidence: 128x2 figures from the 8-seed nondeterministic arm that completed, ledger/gh200-rung0-capacity-sw005-nondet-2026-09-21.jsonl on the box, recipe_hash 97d0f8e2b6, seed 0 line: 'total 2.5863 -> 0.5521 [choice 1.921->0.547 (floor 1.131) span 13.312->0.111]'. 512x6 figures from a 1-seed 1-epoch memory probe, /home/ubuntu/probe-batch.log, which the tool's own collapse gate reported as 'span 31.982 against choice 3.409, a 9.4:1 ratio'. The 256x4 opening values are NOT measured -- that point OOM'd before its first step.
impact: This is the third distinct reason the capacity question has not been answered, and it is the same SHAPE as the first. The 2026-09-20 sweep was invalidated because every point ran at the unweighted sum, inside the regime where the choice head is pinned at the class prior. Fixing that by setting span_weight=0.05 everywhere removes the collapse but does not equalise the objective -- it equalises the COEFFICIENT, which is not the same thing when the quantity it multiplies scales with width. A null from such a sweep cannot distinguish 'capacity does not help' from 'the objective is progressively more misbalanced as capacity rises'.
workaround: Report the opening ratio for every point beside its result, so the confound is visible rather than assumed away. The tool already prints it; nothing reads it back.
action_required: Open, and it is a design decision rather than a bug: either (a) hold the coefficient fixed and report the ratio per point, accepting that the objective differs, or (b) set span_weight per point so the WEIGHTED channels open at a common ratio, which makes the objective comparable and the coefficient not. (b) is defensible only if the normalisation is fixed before the numbers are read, or it becomes a free parameter chosen after seeing which answer is convenient. Neither has been done. Note also that whether the opening imbalance survives training is unmeasured: the 128x2 arm converges span to 0.111, so it may wash out, and the 512x6 collapse observed in the probe is at 1 epoch / 91 steps and is not evidence about 10.

question: GAP-COST-USD-IS-ZERO-ON-EVERY-ROW-EVER-WRITTEN found cost_usd = 0.0 on all 799 rows and blamed RunRecorder's cost_usd_per_hour default. Is that where it starts?
answer: NO, it starts two layers up and is worse than a wrong number in a row. Four tools reached CostEstimate through the same literal -- usd_per_hour=0.0, n_gpus=0, instance=f'local-{device}' -- on EVERY device, so every GH200 run this project has made recorded itself as a local run on zero GPUs at zero dollars an hour. tools/real_ft_run.py:_control's own docstring said what should happen instead: 'a rented machine sets a real rate here and RunControl refuses to start without approved_by'. Nothing enforced it.
evidence: The arithmetic, verified: requires_human_approval is `n_gpus > 1 or projected_usd >= APPROVAL_FREE_USD`. At (0, 0.0) the first disjunct is False and the second is `0.0 * cap_hours >= 20`, False at EVERY cap the program admits including MAX_CAP_S (40 h). And the per-GPU/per-instance column check is gated on `if self.n_gpus > 1`, so it never ran. 10 tests, 8 of them verified to fail against the pre-fix tree; the other two are a characterisation of the defective arithmetic and a control that a local run is still not refused.
impact: One defect -- the tool never saying what machine it is on -- switched off BOTH of rule 4's enforcement mechanisms at once. The human-yes gate could not fire on any run, an 8xH100 block run included; and DESIGN-4's own error, a rate read off the per-GPU column instead of the per-instance one, was unguarded on exactly the multi-GPU jobs the guard exists for. A human approving a full train on the strength of `approval_line()` would have read '0 GPU(s) at $0.00/h ... $0.00 at the cap -- no approval required'.
workaround: CostEstimate.for_device(cap=, device=, ...) is the one owner now. cpu and mps are priced at zero, which is a measured fact about a Mac that is already bought and not a loophole -- refusing to price a local run would push every local caller into inventing a rate, and an invented number in an append-only ledger is permanent. Anything else is rented by the hour and the caller states instance, usd_per_hour and n_gpus or gets a refusal naming all three and the reason. real_ft_run.py takes --instance / --usd-per-hour / --usd-per-gpu-hour / --approved-by, refuses a cuda run without the first two AT ARGV TIME rather than after a 24-second tower load, counts n_gpus with torch.cuda.device_count(), and passes the rate to the recorder so cost_usd is a real duration times a real rate.
action_required: RESOLVED for tools/real_ft_run.py and tools/ft_toy_run.py's owner path. STILL OPEN for tools/rung0_real_run.py and tools/rung0_toy_run.py, which carry the same literal and belong to the concurrent lane -- one of them was mid-sweep on the GH200 when this landed, so changing it under them was refused rather than risked. They have been told the shape and the constructor is theirs to call.

question: Raised by the concurrent lane after measuring the GH200: the box is 8b9df39 plus 72 modified-or-untracked paths and 6894 insertions, so every GPU row's code_commit reads '8b9df39-dirty'. What does that pin?
answer: One bit, for an unbounded amount of divergence, on the rows that carry every training number this project has. The box is synced by COPYING files into a clone pinned at an old commit, so '-dirty' is its normal state rather than an exception -- the suffix is present on every row and distinguishes nothing. The lane's own check resolved well this time (rung0_real_run.py on the box byte-identical to dec1bce by sha256) and the row does not say that, and nothing would have caught it if it had not.
evidence: tools/real_ft_run.py now records a code_that_ran metric on BOTH row kinds: a sha256 over {source: sha256} for all 26 qd_train modules plus the tool itself, with every source named at 7 hex digits in the detail. Measured on this Mac: 26 of 26 sources, digest 72dcf09ae97862ab... 6 tests, 5 of them verified to fail against the pre-fix tree; the sixth is the guard that code_fingerprint()'s zero-argument default still hashes qd_data and nothing else.
impact: For a full train this is the difference between a row that can be reproduced and one that can only be re-attempted. 'something in the tree differs from 8b9df39' is not a provenance record; 'trainer.py is d798f99' is. The fix already existed in this repository -- qd_data/fingerprint.py::code_fingerprint, written for shard headers -- and needed only to be pointed somewhere else.
workaround: code_fingerprint gained an optional directory and is byte-for-byte unchanged with no argument, which matters because every shard set on disk is verified against its zero-argument result at ShardReader.open(). qd_data is deliberately NOT included in code_that_ran: the shard header already fingerprints it and the reader already checks it, and a second owner of one answer is free to disagree with the first.
action_required: RESOLVED for tools/real_ft_run.py. Not done, and a judgement for a human rather than an agent: whether code_commit itself should refuse to write '-dirty' for a run that will cost money. That is a change to what a ledger row means and it belongs with whoever owns the launch procedure, not in a hardening pass.

RESIDUAL, and it is the same defect one layer up: the row's cost_usd comes from RunRecorder.cost_usd_per_hour (ledger.py:955, default 0.0, multiplied at :1092), which no runner but real_ft_run.py passes. So the ESTIMATE is now honest and the ROW is still zero. trainer.py:870 already computes control.cost.cost_for(wall) correctly and puts it in TrainResult rather than the row, so connecting them is a deletion. This lane owns that, sequenced after the audit lane's ledger.py work. DECIDED for rows already written: no correction row. The ledger is append-only, has no supersede/amend mechanism and no 'correction' run kind, so one would be inventing a mechanism rather than using it.
