question: control_key folds a sha256 of python/qd_train/baseline.py into every cache entry, so any edit to that file invalidates every fitted control. What does a cache miss actually cost now that the corpus is commitpackft-sized, and is the digest still the right trade?
answer: It costs 36.5 minutes, and the digest is clearly the right trade. Measured 2026-09-22 by paying it: seven fits (one full-corpus, then holdout+sizematch for three operators), 204.2s to 351.7s each, 2190.4s total, about $0.91. All seven converged at tol in 405-661 iterations. Commit 20cc7f5 moved context_texts into baseline.py -- a pure relocation -- and cold-started all six cached entries; the digest cannot see intent, sees different bytes, and fails closed, which is what it is for. CORRECTION to the first version of this record, which said ~15 hours and ~$22: that came from projected_fit_seconds, which prices max_iter iterations and overshot the measured time by 17.6x. The fit is BLAS-parallel (load 64.8 on 64 cores) and does contend with a GPU arm -- an arm seed ran 215s against 93s uncontended -- but that is a scheduling fact, not a cost of this size.
impact: The digest must NOT be weakened: a cache that survived an edit to the control would serve a verdict from code that no longer exists, and every margin measured against it afterwards would be against an opponent the run never faced. At 36 minutes to rebuild the entire cache that guarantee is nearly free, which is the opposite of the conclusion the first version of this record invited. The residual is about the PROJECTION, not the cache: projected_fit_seconds is a worst-case bound presented like an estimate, and it has now misled three artifacts -- a timeout in fit_operator_holdout_controls.sh was declared fatal when it was not, a running fit was killed about six minutes in on the strength of it (roughly when it would have finished), and a $0.91 job was routed to a human as a $22 spending decision. fit_linear_control.py now documents it as a bound and consumes it only as a refusal precondition, never as a cost. Whether a relocation-only edit should be able to preserve the cache (digesting a normalised AST rather than raw bytes) is a change to what the guarantee MEANS and remains a human's.

question: tools/ledger_arms.py groups rows into arms by (recipe_hash, backbone_commit) and treats every row in a group as a distinct seed. Does any committed ledger put the same protocol.seed into one group twice, and did any reported number pool them?
answer: The first half is answered: yes. Scanned 2026-09-22 over all 27 committed ledgers (1359 rows, every one carrying protocol.seed): 13 files repeat a seed inside a (recipe_hash, backbone_commit) group -- gh200-2026-09-20 (43 repeated group-seeds), gh200-2026-09-21 (53), runs.jsonl (44), gh200-overnight-2026-09-21 (18), gh200-context-source-2026-09-22 (8), gh200-fourway-2026-09-22 (6), gh200-determinism-2026-09-21 (4), gh200-commitpackft-2026-09-22 (3), gh200-det-2026-09-21 (2), gh200-seedcheck-2026-09-21 (2), mac-rung0-prereg-2026-09-21 (2), gh200-rung0-repro-2026-09-21 (1), gh200-rung0-reprodet-2026-09-21 (1). Some are deliberate (the determinism and repro ledgers re-run one seed on purpose); others look like retries at one rev. No file had a duplicated row_id. The second half -- whether any AUDIT or HANDOFF number was computed by ledger_arms over one of these groups -- is NOT answered.
impact: A seed counted twice inflates n and shrinks the spread, and the floor ledger_arms prints is computed from both, so a pooled arm claims more resolving power than it has -- the flattering direction. The same defect in tools/operator_holdout_report.py was fixed in 692c154 (it now refuses, naming the rows), because a re-run was about to make it live there. It was deliberately NOT applied to ledger_arms in the same change: refusing would stop that tool reading 13 existing ledgers, some of which repeat seeds by design, so the right behaviour there (refuse, dedupe to one run, or report per rev) is a decision about those ledgers and not a mechanical port.

question: Does a run killed by SIGTERM write a row that says what code produced it?
answer: Yes, since 2c84587 (2026-09-22 06:20 UTC), and this record was simply never updated. RunRecorder.__enter__ records the what_ran_state digest FIRST, before the signal handlers are installed (python/qd_train/ledger.py, __enter__), so it is on the row whether the block completes, raises, or is killed. Re-verified 2026-09-22 ~20:45 UTC: python/tests/test_provenance_on_every_exit.py passes 7 of 7, including test_a_run_killed_mid_block_still_records_the_digest, which delivers a real SIGTERM to the test process inside the block and asserts the killed row carries the digest; test_every_tool_that_records_a_run_passes_its_entry_point makes a tool that opts out visible. The metric's name now has one owner, qd_train.ledger.CODE_THAT_RAN (c261a6c).
impact: Real rows back the completed path -- all 144 operator-holdout rows carry code_that_ran (5bad419d... for rows 1-72, 7318cbb3... for 73-144). They do not yet back the killed path: no committed ledger has a killed row written after 2c84587 (the 42 non-completed rows all predate it), so that half rests on the test's real SIGTERM. test_ledger_provenance, which found the original defect on an arriving row, is what will see the first real one.

question: Rule 1 sends every navigation question to DevMap first. Can the DevMap MCP tools answer after the index is rebuilt underneath a long-running server?
answer: No, not in this session. From ~20:39 UTC 2026-09-22 every DevMap MCP call -- devmap_search, devmap_status -- returned 'database disk image is malformed', after the same tools answered normally earlier in the session. The store itself was healthy: `sqlite3 -readonly .devmap/codeintel/devmap.sqlite 'PRAGMA quick_check'` returned ok, journal_mode wal, and the devmap CLI (0.2.3) answered `devmap search --root <repo> RunRecorder` correctly from a fresh connection. The store had been rewritten at 20:39 and 20:42 UTC (a rebuild after commits), and devmap.sqlite.writer.lock named PID 57850, which was no longer running. Ten or more `devmap mcp` processes were alive, some for 14+ hours. Inferred, not proven: the MCP server holds a connection opened on the pre-rebuild file and reads the replaced one through stale WAL/shm state.
impact: An agent following rule 1 gets an error rather than an empty answer, which is the better failure -- but an agent that treats the error as 'DevMap unavailable' and greps will not know the CLI still works. Workaround used here: the devmap CLI with --root, labelled as such. Fix is outside this repo (DevMap's server should reopen on a replaced store, or the rebuild should write through SQLite rather than replace the file); the immediate remedy is reconnecting the MCP server, a user action.

question: does apply_remap_to_model preserve the tie, and leave no stale full-vocabulary tensor, on the REAL Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B-Base?
answer: Yes, on the model this repository trains -- measured, not inferred. impact: Two things this row does not cover. (1) The record asked for Qwen3_5ForCausalLM. No training or product path loads that class: devmap neighbors finds apply_remap_to_model's only non-test caller is backbone.remap_text_tower, whose callers are real_ft_run._train and this tool, and rg -uu finds CausalLM loaded only in stack/verify_fast_path.py, which never remaps. The trainer's tower has no lm_head; the tied embedding is the head, passed to fused_linear_cross_entropy. So the lm_head tie the record feared for is not on the training path, and whether an EXPORTED CausalLM keeps it is a question for whoever writes the export. (2) The row is quick=True. Its 79 sequences come from the shard set whose remap is under test (242 of 321 were over the 2 GiB logit cap or under 2 tokens), so held-out coverage -- the other half of the plan's parity gate -- is not measured.

question: The memory budget is 480,323,584 parameters smaller when the remap is applied. Is that saving real, and how large is it exactly?
answer: The vocabulary half is now MEASURED on the real checkpoint, not just arithmetic. impact: Budget the remapped vocabulary as real from now on: 7.16 GiB of static state at 16 bytes per parameter is measured, not an upside. The master-copy term still has to be budgeted at its larger value until the optimizer decision is made.
action_required: Vocabulary half: none. Optimizer half: a human states whether fp32 master weights are kept -- tools/real_ft_run.py --optimizer takes 'bf16' (the default, 8 B/param) or 'master' (fp32 master and moments, 20 B/param) -- and then this closes.

question: The remap keeps every token the TRAIN rows use and nothing else, and RemapTable.encode raises on any other id (no UNK, by qd_train.remap's stated policy). How many val and held-out rows can it encode at all?
answer: Almost none. Under the 27,595-id remap built from 3364 train rows: val 5 of 184 rows encodable -- 179 hold at least one dropped id, 3,210 of 103,035 tokens, 644 distinct ids; held-out 124 of 2,109 -- 1,985 hold one, 12,208 of 971,897 tokens, 1,174 distinct ids. Only 1-3% of TOKENS are missing, but rows run to hundreds of tokens, so nearly every ROW holds one, and one is enough for encode to refuse the row. Nothing had measured this because the pipeline never tokenized either split: the remap is built from the train census and only train shards are written.
impact: Final-train blocking for evaluation and serving, not for training. (1) The plan's S2 gate -- loss on held-out sequences under the remap -- cannot be run on 94% of held-out rows; row af64957d passed it only on sequences the remap was built from. (2) Every held-out gate (conformal coverage, abstain rate, kappa, ECE) needs the model to score held-out rows, and under this remap it cannot see 94% of them. (3) The same policy at serve time refuses any input holding one token the training corpus never used, which is most real inputs. Training itself is unaffected: every train row encodes by construction.
workaround: None applied; the no-UNK policy is deliberate and documented, so changing it is a design decision. The options, none yet measured for cost: (a) build the remap over a corpus wider than the train split -- the full commitpackft download, or train + val (val is a TRAINING_SPLITS member) -- which raises coverage but never to 100%; building it over held-out text would make a training artifact depend on held-out data (rule 3). (b) A byte fallback: always keep Qwen's byte-level base tokens and re-segment an unkept token into kept pieces. Feasible: the tokenizer is a ByteLevel BPE (Qwen2Tokenizer, byte_fallback false) and all 256 byte symbols are single tokens in its 248,077-token vocabulary, checked 2026-09-22 against the cached snapshot. That is lossless -- the bytes are the text, unlike an UNK -- and encode can then never refuse, at the cost of longer sequences for rare tokens and a segmentation the base model never saw for them. (c) No remap: the full 248,320-row head, giving up the 480,323,584-parameter saving row af64957d measured.
action_required: Choose (a), (b) or (c) before the final train: it decides which shard sets can be evaluated and what the runtime can serve. The agent side can then measure the chosen option's coverage and cost with the same stage 5b.

question: tools/ledger_arms.py keys an arm on (recipe_hash, backbone_commit), plus the code digest under --split-by-code. Each row's protocol also carries data_snapshot_hash and tokenizer_hash. Should they be part of an arm's identity?
answer: Not answered, and latent in the committed rows. A scan of every tracked ledger on 2026-09-22 found one (recipe_hash, backbone_commit) group whose measured rows span two data snapshots: ledger/mac-rung0-prereg-2026-09-21.jsonl, a 4-row CPU check of the pre-registration flags. Its two runs were launched at 417413c and 0e897b3 and read snapshots c2e856e15a and 6267ab7c85. Every other measured arm in every tracked ledger has one data snapshot and one tokenizer. That ledger repeats seeds 0 and 1, so since dd59c68 ledger_arms refuses it. It refuses with or without --split-by-code, because both runs carry one code digest, and the refusal names both snapshots. Nothing catches the same split with DISJOINT seeds: two snapshots under one recipe and backbone, each seed once, pooled into one arm without a word.
impact: An arm that pools two training corpora reports their difference as seed spread. Unlike a repeated seed this does not inflate n, so it widens the floor rather than flattering it. It is still not one population, and the report does not say so. The likely fix is to key an arm on the protocol minus its seed. On every clean ledger that changes nothing, but it changes what an arm's label must show.

question: tools/ledger_arms.py groups rows into arms by (recipe_hash, backbone_commit) and treats every row in a group as a distinct seed. Does any committed ledger put the same protocol.seed into one group twice, and did any reported number pool them?
answer: Both halves answered. (1) Of the 13 ledgers that repeat a protocol.seed inside a (recipe_hash, backbone_commit) group, 6 repeat it among rows ledger_arms MEASURES (rows carrying both val_choice_top1_over_baseline and train_choice_top1_over_train_majority): gh200-fourway-2026-09-22 (5 seeds), gh200-context-source-2026-09-22 (8), gh200-commitpackft-2026-09-22 (3), mac-rung0-prereg-2026-09-21 (2), gh200-rung0-repro-2026-09-21 (1) and gh200-rung0-reprodet-2026-09-21 (1). The other 7 repeat only on build, smoke, verdict, memorise and killed rows, which enter no sample. (2) Every ledger an AUDIT or HANDOFF file reads WITH ledger_arms is clean: capacity-4096-e10/e30, sw005-nondet, learning-curve-2026-09-21, curve-n24 and span-in-diff. The tool's output on each is byte-identical before and after the fix. The numbers that pooled a repeated seed were computed by hand over the same grouping. They sit in HANDOFF/context-source-2026-09-22.md's four-way table and the gap it opened. The `after` row is n=13, which is 8 seeds; complete-run figures follow in brackets. Margin -0.0764 (-0.0774), 0/13 positive (0/8), top-1 50.20% (50.10%). Span start '1.50% over 13 rows' is 1.49% over 8, still below the 3.2% chance; GAP-RUNG0-SPAN-HEAD-COLLAPSES-WHEN-IT-MUST-ALSO-ABSTAIN repeats that figure. The '29 completed rows' matches neither the 37 margin rows nor the 32 distinct seeds. Its '+4.1%' was already the complete run's figure. Outside AUDIT and HANDOFF, b72aa54's commit message gives the width-128 commitpackft arm as 'val 50.18%'. That equals what ledger_arms prints for the pooled 11 rows over 8 seeds; the complete run is 50.29%. AUDIT/capacity-and-learning-rate.md's '3.9 points' matches the complete run (3.87), not the pooled 3.76. The pooled four-way read printed sd 0.60pp and an honest one-sample floor of 0.51pp. The complete run's own are 0.76pp and 0.87pp: pooling claimed about 1.7x the resolution. No conclusion changes. Every margin, pooled or not, is negative, and the span head is below chance on every seed.
impact: A seed counted twice inflates n and shrinks the spread, and the floor ledger_arms prints is computed from both, so a pooled arm claims more resolving power than it has -- the flattering direction. The same defect in tools/operator_holdout_report.py was fixed in 692c154 (it now refuses, naming the rows), because a re-run was about to make it live there. It was deliberately NOT applied to ledger_arms in the same change: refusing would stop that tool reading 13 existing ledgers, some of which repeat seeds by design, so the right behaviour there (refuse, dedupe to one run, or report per rev) is a decision about those ledgers and not a mechanical port.
fix: dd59c68: ledger_arms refuses a seed measured twice in one arm with RepeatedSeed, naming both rows with their code digest, data snapshot and write time. --split-by-code reads one arm per code version: the code_that_ran digest, else the launch rev. Not per rev alone, because all three re-runs share their launch rev with the run they repeat. Not dedupe, because keep-first would have built the four-way arm from two code versions and keep-last rewards re-running. The two repro pairs stay refused under the flag: one seed twice at one code is a reproducibility check, not a population. Repeats on unmeasured rows are counted and said, not refused. The repeat rule and code_of have one owner, ledger_arms.SeedClaims, which operator_holdout_report imports; that report's output is byte-identical on its committed ledger. HANDOFF/context-source-2026-09-22.md carries two 'Corrected 2026-09-22' notes.
residual: GAP-LEDGER-ARMS-KEY-OMITS-THE-DATA-SNAPSHOT: an arm spanning two data snapshots with disjoint seeds is still pooled silently. GAP-RUNG0-SPAN-HEAD-COLLAPSES-WHEN-IT-MUST-ALSO-ABSTAIN (owner human) still reads '1.50% over 13 rows'. This lane left that for its owner rather than re-appending someone else's record. b72aa54's message cannot be amended.

tool: tools/real_tokenizer_pipeline.py stage 5b (cbcbff6); ledger/mac-shards-commitpackft-2026-09-22.jsonl row 1a1f7d67-c480-464e-acfd-5180287651fe, metrics remap_byte_fallback_val_tokens and remap_byte_fallback_heldout_tokens, beside d9b461ca's coverage counts
question: What does option (b), the lossless byte fallback, cost on the rows the train remap cannot encode?
answer: Little. Spelling every dropped token in single-byte tokens adds at most 15,368 tokens to val's 103,035 (14.92%, re-spelling 3,210 tokens) and at most 66,045 to held-out's 971,897 (6.80%, re-spelling 12,208). These are upper bounds: re-segmenting into the longest kept pieces is never longer. The remap already keeps 126 of the 256 byte tokens, so a fallback adds 130 embedding rows to 27,595. The coverage counts are unchanged from d9b461ca: val 5 of 184 rows encodable, held-out 124 of 2,109. The two rows share a protocol hash and every other value.
impact: Option (b) costs 130 rows and at most about 7-15% longer sequences on unseen text, against option (c)'s 480,323,584 parameters, and against option (a), which cannot reach 100% without held-out text. What (b) does not price is quality: a dropped token re-spelled in bytes is a segmentation the base model never saw for that string, and whether that costs accuracy is a model measurement, not a count.
action_required: Unchanged: choose (a), (b) or (c). If (b), the agent-side work is a fallback in RemapTable.encode's caller -- never an UNK -- plus the 256 byte ids forced into the kept set, and qd_train.remap's coverage-policy docstring amended to say why.

question: The plan's final train is an 8xH100 block. What in this repository drives more than one GPU?
answer: Nothing. rg -uu finds no DistributedDataParallel, FSDP, torchrun, init_process_group, world_size or LOCAL_RANK in any code; the only hits are HANDOFF/memory-2026-09-20.md, HANDOFF/costctl-2026-09-20.md and a comment in tools/memory_budget.py, each saying there is none. train_ft takes no device argument -- the device belongs to the caller's TrainStep -- and every tool that trains picks one device. RunControl and CostEstimate price n_gpus correctly, so an 8-GPU job would be priced as eight while one of them trained.
impact: An 8xH100 block launched on this code buys seven idle GPUs. It is also the whole of rule 4's multi-GPU case: requires_human_approval is always true above one GPU, so the approval would be for silicon nothing uses.
workaround: Two layouts, and choosing is a cost decision: (a) data-parallel -- one run across eight GPUs, which needs DDP or FSDP wiring through TrainStep, the sampler (each rank a disjoint slice of ShardReader's deterministic order) and Checkpoint (rank-0 writes, all ranks resume at one consumed_digest); or (b) seed-parallel -- eight independent single-GPU runs, one seed per GPU, which needs only a launcher and satisfies rule 8's three-seed floor in one wall-clock slot. (b) is small; (a) is the only way one run gets faster.
action_required: Choose (a) or (b). The agent side then builds it and measures it on the box before an 8-GPU hour is spent.

question: The plan is CPT then FT. What runs qd_train.trainer.train_cpt on the real model?
answer: Nothing outside the tests. devmap neighbors train_cpt lists callers only in python/tests/test_trainer.py and test_fused_ce.py; rg -uu over tools/, python/qd_train, stack/ and crates/ finds the definition and no call. The loop itself is built and tested (resume, checkpoint, accumulation, exhaustion), and QwenDecisionStep satisfies both trainer protocols (test_backbone). What is missing is the driver: a tool that loads the tower, remaps it, builds CPT batches -- Batch with all three supervision fields None -- from a CPT shard set, and records a row.
impact: The final train's first stage cannot be run. FT alone can, on the real model, which is what every FT row so far measures.
workaround: Two pieces, and one is not an agent's: the CPT corpus (docs/plan-corrections.md: AgentPack is gated and cannot be the unattended CPT corpus; commitpackft is the primary licence-filtered pool) and the remap it is built under (GAP-REMAP-CANNOT-ENCODE-THE-ROWS-IT-WAS-NOT-BUILT-FROM). The driver itself is agent work once those are fixed.
action_required: Name the CPT corpus and settle the remap question; then an agent builds tools/real_cpt_run.py on the real_ft_run pattern and smokes it on one GPU.

tool: RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH= rg -uu over the tree (.git, target, .venv, *.jsonl excluded) and devmap neighbors (CLI; the MCP server reads the store as malformed, GAP-DEVMAP-MCP-READS-A-REPLACED-STORE-AS-MALFORMED), 2026-09-22; tools/real_ft_run.py read: _evaluate scores the batches it trained on
question: Every plan gate is measured on held-out data. What scores a fine-tuned 2B on rows it did not train on?
answer: Nothing. tools/real_ft_run.py's _evaluate is a no-grad pass over its own training plan -- the memorisation floor, which is what that tool claims -- and the eval harness (qd_train.eval_harness.evaluate) has one caller, tools/rung0_real_run.py, the byte-level rung-0 model. The pipeline writes train shards only; val and held-out exist as manifests. And the remap is built from the train rows alone, so under it 5 of 184 val rows and 124 of 2,109 held-out rows can be encoded at all (row d9b461ca).
impact: No rung-3 number so far says anything about generalisation, and none can until this exists: every FT row is a memorisation or single-epoch row on its own training rows. The final train would have no held-out result to gate on.
workaround: The val half is agent work that changes no policy: val is in TRAINING_SPLITS, so the remap may be built over train + val and val shards written through the training door; real_ft_run then needs an arm that scores those shards (letter top-1 over each row's own options against the majority class, span top-1). The held-out half waits on GAP-REMAP-CANNOT-ENCODE-THE-ROWS-IT-WAS-NOT-BUILT-FROM, since a held-out row the remap cannot encode cannot be scored.
action_required: Build the val half (pipeline --val-shards, a real_ft_run scoring arm) and run it on the box; the held-out half follows the remap decision.

question: tools/operator_holdout_report.py groups rows into cells by (operator, condition), deliberately not by rev. Should a cell also be keyed on the protocol's data_snapshot_hash and tokenizer_hash, as ledger_arms's arms are since c448560?
answer: Not answered here. The report shares SeedClaims with ledger_arms, so a seed repeated in a cell is refused, but two runs of one cell over two data snapshots with disjoint seeds would pool into one population without a word: the defect GAP-LEDGER-ARMS-KEY-OMITS-THE-DATA-SNAPSHOT closed in ledger_arms. Latent: every measured row of the committed ledger/gh200-operator-holdout-model-2026-09-22.jsonl reads snapshot 728eee3743 and tokenizer bytes-utf8-256, so keying on them changes nothing there. Left unchanged in c448560 because a live lane reads this report and its output had to stay byte-identical, which it does on all 29 committed ledgers.

question: Without --split-by-code, ledger_arms names an arm that mixes code versions (ARM RAN DIFFERENT CODE) but says nothing when two arms each ran one code and the two differ. Should an arm-vs-arm line say so, as it says since c448560 when it crosses a data snapshot or a tokenizer?
answer: Not answered; measured. In ledger/gh200-rung0-curve-n24-2026-09-22.jsonl, which HANDOFF/coordinator-2026-09-21.md and HANDOFF/coordinator-fork-2026-09-21.md read with this tool, 7 of the 10 arm-vs-arm lines compare arms whose code_that_ran digests differ. The three curve points (train_subsample 1.0, 0.5, 0.25) share fdec48ce5b4bd33d, so the curve's own three comparisons do not cross code; recipes 991b57587f and d6248d9dd9 (subsample 1.0 each) ran 298481c04273352b and 20f9156afe0045d0. Read with ledger_arms, gh200-operator-holdout-model has 81 of 153 such lines; AUDIT/operator-holdout-model.md already names its two digests and reads it with operator_holdout_report, which prints ARMS RAN DIFFERENT CODE. With --split-by-code every label names its code, so the crossing is visible there. Whether any of these code differences touched the computation was not established: a code_that_ran digest changes with any imported file.
impact: A difference across code versions includes whatever the change did, while the line reads as the recipe's or the backbone's alone. Extending ledger_arms._crossed to name a code crossing is a few lines, but it adds a note to 7 lines of curve-n24's documented output, which c448560 was asked to keep byte-identical -- so it is a decision, not a drive-by.

question: ledger_arms._spread prints 'smallest visible difference ... 0.00 / 0.00pp' for a sample whose seeds all scored the same. Should a zero estimated sd print a floor at all?
answer: Not answered. One committed ledger has such a sample: mac-rung0-prereg, readable since c448560. Each of its two arms has two collapsed seeds at exactly 48.86%, so 'all seeds: n=2 ... sd 0.00pp' is followed by floors of 0.00pp, split or not. Checked over all 58 reads of the 29 committed ledgers at 64052f4 (51 read, 7 refused). The same display appeared before dd59c68, when the four rows pooled as one arm. The arm is flagged COLLAPSED with fitted n=0 beside it, so no reading uses it today.
impact: A floor of zero claims the arm can see any difference at all: the flattering direction, and the limiting case of the module docstring's warning that a collapsed arm's tight sd looks like precision. Primed as a prior, that sd would claim unlimited sensitivity.

answer: No. From about 17:10 -0500 on 2026-09-22, devmap_search failed 3 times and one devmap_explore once with 'fts5: corruption found reading blob 412316860426 from table "nodes_fts"', the last after the store's 17:13-17:15 write; two later devmap_explore calls failed with 'database disk image is malformed'. devmap_explore had answered for arms_of and SeedClaims earlier in the same session, and devmap_neighbors on an exact symbol id still answered. devmap_status meanwhile reported only degraded_reason 'source tree differs from the indexed generation' (generation 2384, 8 files changed, quarantined 0) and nothing about corruption. A read-only PRAGMA quick_check on .devmap/codeintel/devmap.sqlite returned ok, so the damage is inside the FTS5 index rather than the b-tree; FTS5's own integrity-check needs a writable handle and was not run. Not repaired: every session in this worktree shares the store, and a writer held devmap.sqlite.writer.lock.

question: tools/ledger_arms.py keys an arm on (recipe_hash, backbone_commit), plus the code digest under --split-by-code. Each row's protocol also carries data_snapshot_hash and tokenizer_hash. Should they be part of an arm's identity?
answer: Yes: an arm is the protocol minus its seed. qd_train.ledger.Protocol.hash_without_seed already names that set as the seed family three rows must share to promote, and a population of seeds is exactly that. Keyed on (recipe_hash, backbone_commit), two data snapshots with disjoint seeds pooled into one arm with nothing refused. The brief's claim that the wider key prints byte-identical output on every ledger but mac-rung0-prereg was checked, not assumed, and it is one ledger short. Over the 29 ledgers as committed at 64052f4, frozen and read by the pre-fix tool and the fixed one with and without --split-by-code, 50 of 58 runs are byte-identical, including both reads of all six documented ledgers. The 8 that differ: mac-rung0-prereg (refused, now two arms of two collapsed seeds, one per snapshot); gh200-2026-09-21 (38 arms, now 39: five unmeasured smoke rows of recipe 5c08c0aa4f on backbone b1485b2fa6 read two snapshots, 4 at fe79253cd2 and 1 at 101168a900, which the earlier scan missed by counting measured rows only); gh200-rung0-repro and -reprodet (still refused, minus the stale 'where the snapshots differ' sentence). tools/operator_holdout_report.py is byte-identical on all 29.
impact: An arm that pooled two training corpora reported their difference as seed spread. It widened the floor rather than flattering it, but it was not one population and the report did not say so.
fix: c448560: ArmKey is a NamedTuple of recipe_hash, backbone_commit, data_snapshot_hash, tokenizer_hash and, under --split-by-code, the code; test_the_arm_key_is_the_writers_protocol_minus_its_seed holds its protocol fields equal to Protocol's minus the seed. A label names the snapshot or the tokenizer only where arms sharing a backbone, a recipe and a code differ in it -- the tokenizer whole, since two tokenizer names can share any prefix -- and an arm-vs-arm line that crosses a snapshot or a tokenizer says ACROSS DATA SNAPSHOTS or ACROSS TOKENIZERS on the line. That note is what makes the narrow label safe: the rung-0 sweeps read 22f39f9d10 and the tuned-capacity, lr-sweep and span-in-diff sweeps 728eee3743, so two ledgers read together otherwise compare across data under labels naming only backbone and recipe. 7 new test items, 6 of which fail against the pre-fix code; the seventh guards against naming a snapshot where it tells nothing apart.
residual: GAP-OPERATOR-HOLDOUT-CELLS-OMIT-THE-DATA-SNAPSHOT: the same omission in tools/operator_holdout_report.py, left unchanged so its output stays byte-identical for the lane that reads it. Found while verifying and not caused by this change: GAP-LEDGER-ARMS-PAIRWISE-SILENT-WHEN-ARMS-RAN-DIFFERENT-CODE and GAP-LEDGER-ARMS-ZERO-SD-PRINTS-A-ZERO-FLOOR.

question: Why did devmap_search and devmap_explore fail in this lane with 'fts5: corruption found reading blob 412316860426 from table "nodes_fts"' and 'database disk image is malformed', and why did devmap_status report only a stale index?
answer: Revised about 17:25 -0500: the store was not corrupt, and the failure was per process, not per worktree. The first record's 'for every session in this worktree' was inferred from this session alone and is withdrawn. Evidence: (1) a fresh read-only sqlite connection to .devmap/codeintel/devmap.sqlite (inode 602540831) reads generation 2433, built 17:18:43 from 2237aca; an FTS MATCH for append_gap returns 2 rows and quick_check is ok. (2) From this same session the GitPulse plugin's devmap_search answers (python/qd_train/gaps.py:147-163) and its devmap_status reports generation 2433, 5215 symbols, 16826 edges. (3) This session's own `devmap mcp` server (pid 33291, child of the session's claude pid 33267, started 16:49:40) still reports generation 2384 and still fails both calls. (4) lsof +L1 shows pid 33291 holding devmap.sqlite-wal and -shm inodes 628008899/628008900 with link count 0 -- deleted while open -- where the files at those paths are now inodes 628065001/628065002. Two other long-lived `devmap mcp` servers on this store hold deleted copies too: pid 36598 (session socket 36574, started 16:15:32) and pid 83988 (session socket 83844, started 15:11:34); whether their queries fail was not checked. The branch-merge session (socket 90712) runs no long-lived server on this store and reads 2433. A connection whose -wal/-shm were unlinked keeps a private WAL index, stops seeing other processes' commits and reads a main file rewritten under it, which fits both errors and the frozen generation. What unlinked the files while connections held them was not established.
impact: A long-lived `devmap mcp` whose WAL files were unlinked answers name lookups with corruption errors -- and, inferred rather than observed, could answer from a stale generation without any error -- while its devmap_status reports only 'source tree differs from the indexed generation' at the frozen generation. Status cannot tell a broken reader from a stale index, and 49 rebuilds (2384 to 2433) never reached these processes. Workaround: restart the affected session's devmap server, or use the GitPulse plugin's devmap_* tools, which read the current store. The fix belongs in DevMap (DevCouncil rust/devmap-store and devmap-serve): do not unlink -wal/-shm under live connections, and make status detect a reader whose WAL files are unlinked or whose generation lags the store's.

question: Why did devmap_search and devmap_explore fail in this lane with 'fts5: corruption found reading blob 412316860426 from table "nodes_fts"' and 'database disk image is malformed' while the store was healthy, and why can a server in that state report itself through devmap_status as merely stale?
answer: The store was never corrupt; long-lived `devmap mcp` servers read it through -wal/-shm files deleted while they held them, and this is not specific to this worktree. Evidence, 2026-09-22 about 17:10-17:30 -0500: (1) a fresh read-only connection to .devmap/codeintel/devmap.sqlite reads generation 2433 (built 17:18:43 from 2237aca), its FTS MATCH answers and quick_check is ok; the GitPulse plugin's devmap_* tools read 2433 and answer from the same session. (2) This session's server (pid 33291, started 16:49:40) stays at generation 2384: devmap_search fails with the fts5 'corruption' error, devmap_explore with 'malformed', and devmap_status reports only a stale index. (3) It also answers devmap_neighbors on tools/ledger_arms.py::arms_of cleanly -- resolution Available, not truncated, confidence 1.0 -- without the arms_of -> _stem and arms_of -> ArmKey edges that c448560 added and the plugin returns: a wrong answer with no error. (4) lsof +L1 shows five `devmap mcp` processes holding deleted -wal/-shm across three stores: 33291, 36598 (started 16:15:32) and 83988 (15:11:34) on this store; 39007 (11:36:48) on /Users/bharath/Code/devtools/GitPulse/.devcouncil/codeintel; 93742 (15:15:38) on /Users/bharath/Code/devtools/gusset/.devcouncil/codeintel. The cross-repo scope was first reported by the branch-merge session and re-checked here. (5) Deletion is intermittent, not per write: this store's current -wal (inode 628065001) survived writes at 17:24-17:26, truncated to 0 bytes by checkpoints rather than recreated, while the deleted inodes the three servers here hold (627810811, 627930158, 628008899) date at least three separate deletions since 15:11. (6) Status differs by server: this one reports merely stale, while the sessions owning 36598 and 83988 report devmap_status itself failing with 'database disk image is malformed' (relayed by the branch-merge session, not observed here). So one condition surfaces three ways: a clean answer from a frozen graph, a status that reads merely stale, or a hard error. The id's 'says only stale' names the second; the status half stays open because status can report it that way. Those two sessions also report that no deletion or retirement of theirs rested on a stale answer (36598: every DevMap query it made predates dd59c68, whose deletions it re-checked with rg -uu; 83988: its commits since about 17:10 are additive). The first record's 'for every session in this worktree' was inferred from one session and is withdrawn. What deletes the files under live connections was not established.

impact: Installing a qd-calib-fit table as-is disables span answers (defect_span), the half of the defect contract that points at lines. Fail-closed, not silent, but it blocks shipping a fitted table for the full schema.

question: When a runtime is built with a fitted CalibrationTable, does a caller's expect.calibration_hash pin that table?
answer: No. check_hashes compares expect.calibration_hash with backend.identity().calibration_hash -- the hash the backend DECLARES -- not with self.calibration.hash(), the table the runtime calibrates with, and Runtime::with_backend never checks that the two agree. ReferenceBackend declares CalibrationTable::reference().hash(); qd-metal declares whatever string its config carries. Measured: a runtime built with a fitted table and the reference backend answers a request pinning the REFERENCE table's hash and refuses one pinning the FITTED table's hash with hash_mismatch -- the pin passes for a table that is not the one serving. One name, two quantities, again.
impact: Latent until a fitted table is served: then a caller pinning the hash qd-calib-fit reports is refused, and a caller pinning the stale declared hash is answered with a different table. Approved means unexamined.
workaround: Not fixed here: it changes the runtime's hash-binding contract (runtime.rs, and the backend identity's meaning), which is a security-adjacent change to ask about, and serve.rs/service.rs carry another editor's uncommitted work. Candidate fix: assemble() refuses a backend whose declared calibration_hash differs from calibration.hash(), or check_hashes reads calibration.hash() directly.

question: Item 6 (N-tower serving): the runtime holds N towers (qd_runtime::ensemble::EnsembleBackend, Runtime::from_ensemble, release::Ensemble, qd-export-ensemble) without serve.rs/service.rs. What is not done, and what would finish it?
answer: (1) No binary serves a Release or an Ensemble on Metal. `qd` (qd-runtime) cannot link MetalBackend: qd-metal depends on qd-runtime. The hook is a binary that links qd-metal: Ensemble::open(dir); for each tower MetalBackend::start(MetalConfig { snapshot: Some(tower.dir()), calibration_hash: ensemble.calibration().hash(), .. }); Runtime::from_ensemble(&ensemble, members, registry, caps); then the existing serve loop. No change to MetalBackend is needed for this: its label_set_hash carries the letter ids, which EnsembleBackend::new compares. (2) Latency of three 2B towers at 8K was not measured: the Mac is shared with sibling lanes running suites, about 16 GB was free against roughly 12 GB of bf16 weights for three towers plus state, and a timing under that contention is not a measurement. Members are prefilled in turn, so the expected cost is the sum of three single-tower prefills; Fable's ~3 s at MLX's 7.6k tok/s is inferred and is MLX's rate, not tessl's. (3) The Python gate rows that score the ensemble must compute qd_runtime::release::ENSEMBLE_DECODE (mean of per-row log-softmax; softmax of it equals softmax of the mean logits) or the gate measures another model than the one served. (4) trained_width is operator-stated with a cited source because nothing upstream records it.
impact: the ensemble is servable through the library and its refusals are tested on CPU; no request is answered by three real towers until (1) lands, and its latency is unknown until (2) runs.

question: Which choices did L-waiters make where the brief or the plans left room?
answer:
Six readings, each for the lead to confirm or strike:
(1) fsucc runs F's CPU linear controls after F' GPU work and after releasing gpu.lock (fsuccgpu.done), so j5pp does not wait on them.
(2) fsucc waits at most 7,200 s for '=== F controls all done' after rungd and j6ctl finish. It then writes refused (exit 3), never quiet.
(3) cudadev caps each device test at 150 s, runga at 300 s and GDN at 600 s, within a 1,500 s total. The device-test HANDOFFs say 900 s; the brief's <= 1,800 s and < $1 binds.
(4) cudadev sets NVIDIA_TF32_OVERRIDE=0 for every binary, not only runga.
(5) j6a refuses a data dir holding data/heldout, and requires the attestation's replay_rows_checked == replay_rows_total (the plan's decontam-2 criteria).
(6) j6a's needle-control argv is not preluded, because it needs the checkpoint training writes. The plan preludes both argvs.
resolution: The lead confirmed all six readings on 2026-10-02 ~04:00 UTC, before launch. (1) F's CPU controls run after F' releases gpu.lock. (2) The wait for F's controls is bounded at 7,200 s, after which the run is refused, never quiet. (3) Caps of 150/300/600 s per binary inside a 1,500 s total, which the brief's 1,800 s / $1 bound allows. (4) TF32 is off for every binary. (5) j6a refuses held-out data in its data dir and an incomplete attestation. (6) j6a's needle-control argv is not preluded.

question: Can J6(a), run untouched from qd-lane8 at a502670, print replay_log for its first and last 20 replay steps beside the concurrent CE? campaign/j6a-preregistered.json arm.replay_flags.report_only_requirement asks for it, and the lead asked the waiter to grep for it.
answer:
No (verified by read):
- PriorKLReplay keeps replay_log in memory only (python/qd_train/replay.py:478, :499).
- The printed report carries only replayed, replay_kl_first and replay_kl_last (tools/real_ft_run.py:2457-2459, printed at :8825).
- state() persists counts, not the log (replay.py:517-528).
- The checkpoint loss_log is the per-optimizer-step loss without the replay term (inferred from replay.py:503-511).
box_q_j6a.sh prints what the run does emit: those keys, the loss_log first and last 20, and the replay counters. It logs that the requirement is NOT MET by this run. It does not branch on any of it, and it wires no observer.
The decision is the lead's or Fable's, before J6(a) launches. The options are:
(a) accept first/last plus loss_log;
(b) a print-only observer around main(), which leaves the ft row recording code_commit a502670 for a process that ran a502670 plus a patch;
(c) amend the pre-registration.
Separately, the pre-registration cites 'a502670 tools/real_ft_run.py:9191-9192' for the missing --replay-weight default. At a502670 those lines are :7818-7819; :9191-9192 is main's (git show). That needs an amendment.
resolution: The lead's ruling, 2026-10-02: accept what a502670 prints, which is the replay count and the first and last replay values (real_ft_run.py:2457-2459, printed at :8825). Patching an observer in would leave the ft row's code_commit naming code that did not run. The requirement is report-only, with no kill criterion, so nothing reads it. Recorded as readings.R3_replay_log in campaign/j6a-preregistered.json, which Fable or the human may strike before J6(a)'s eval row.

question: Does word 8-gram containment >= 0.5 over rendered prompt_content (qd_train.replay.decontaminate's definition, which Fable's v5 rule keeps unchanged) find real overlap in every family, or does each family's constant question make short rows hit each other?
answer: For CLINC it is mostly the question. prompt_content keeps the question, and every intent.* row of a family carries the same one (e.g. 'Is the utterance in scope for the assistant at all?', 11 words, 4 whole 8-grams) before a short utterance and two option words. A val row of 18 words has 11 grams; any train utterance that starts with the same one or two words ('what is') shares 5-6 of them and is excluded. Example from the 5% scan: train 'what is the minimum payment on my eddie bauer card' and 'what is the calorie going to be if i'm eating cereal' both hit val 'what is spanish for hello' (5 of 10 grams). CLINC identity keys are shared by all four intent families, so one hit drops the utterance from all four. The share of CLINC train utterance keys excluded grows with the sample: 8.5% at 1%, 9.1% at 2%, 20.1% at 5% (more targets per source); at full scale it is likely much higher. MMLU 5.9-6.9%, code.defect_class 0.8-1.1%, CSQA and SQuAD answer_span 0%. Not changed here: the brief and the ruling fix the definition, n and threshold. The choice (context and options only for families whose question is constant, a per-family exemption, or accept the exclusion) is the human's, before the full v5 list is applied.

question: Are the containment scan's source texts the text the model trains on?
answer: Not exactly. tools/containment_scan.py renders every row (train sources and val/held-out targets alike) through replay_decontam.row_texts: render(row.request, seed=None), then prompt_content. That is the oracle path and replay_decontam's target path, so both sides of the scan are consistent with each other. The shards are rendered at config.seed, which can permute a row's options; an 8-gram that spans an option boundary can differ between the scanned text and the trained text. Question and context grams are unaffected. Not measured: how many pairs would change if sources were rendered at the shard seed.

question: qd-prep containment has no dependency for Python's re \w and str.lower(). Does it match the oracle for every input?
answer: It carries tables generated from CPython 3.14 (Unicode 16.0.0): \w membership, lower() mappings including multi-code-point ones, and the Final_Sigma context classes, in crates/qd-prep/src/pyunicode_tables.rs. --check passes under both 3.14 interpreters and the generator test is skipped, with the reason, on any other Unicode version. Code points unassigned (Cn) in 16.0 are refused rather than guessed. Between 15.1.0 and 16.0.0: no \w or lower() difference on code points assigned in 15.1; U+1171E's category change moves its sigma class; 5,185 code points are newly assigned in 16.0.
residual: Parity is exact against a Python on Unicode 16.0.0. An oracle run on 15.1 (the repo .venv) can differ on texts holding U+1171E next to a capital sigma, or any of the 5,185 newly assigned code points; qd-prep accepts those, so such a difference would not be refused. A future Python on another Unicode version needs the tables regenerated (the --check test then fails or skips).

A val row of 18 words has 11 grams; any train utterance that starts with the same one or two words ('what is') shares 5-6 of them and is excluded. The share of CLINC train utterance keys excluded grows with the sample: 8.5% at 1%, 9.1% at 2%, 20.1% at 5% (more targets per source); at full scale it is likely much higher. MMLU 5.9-6.9%, code.defect_class 0.8-1.1%, CSQA and SQuAD answer_span 0%. Not changed here: the brief and the ruling fix the definition, n and threshold. The choice (context and options only for families whose question is constant, a per-family exemption, or accept the exclusion) is the human's, before the full v5 list is applied.

answer: [V, by reading] It answers it. The admission check (admission.rs:42, 55-60) runs only when task == code.defect_class. answer: [V] The request (QDPMHIN1) carries every distinct row's whitespace-token 5-shingles as bytes, so each word travels about five times. The v5 scan's request was 4,534,193,280 bytes, past qd-prep's old 4 GiB bound, and the scan stopped (20:06Z 2026-10-03). The Python process held 17.4 GB RSS at that stage (24.3 GB peak footprint). The bound went to 16 GiB in v5-build ca48960 (Fable's ruling: raise, do not chunk). [I] The class fix is Rust-side shingling: send each row's text once, shingle in qd-prep with a parity test against the Python reference's shingles (the canaries already compare signatures). That shrinks the request ~5x, takes the shingling loop out of Python, and lowers the Mac's peak RSS.
impact: Every pool-reading build and every split rebuild on the box ships ~5x more bytes than it needs and shingles in Python. The Mac build sits closer to mac_heavy's 32 GiB RSS cap than it would otherwise. A v6 Rust-port target (the human's 'minimize python bottlenecks with rust'); not done in v5, whose data code is frozen for the pre-registration.

question: What does real_ft_run.optimizer_spec do with a recipe name it does not know?

question: Can the Rust trainer (qd-train over tessl, or ojas) train with bf16 weights and a smaller optimizer state?

owner: the human (upstream report to github.com/Mapika/decider is his call)
finding: Root cause measured on this Mac (torch 2.12.1, transformers 5.12.1, M5 Pro), under tools/mac_heavy.sh. (1) The model is not at fault: decider_mps_bisect.py ran decider's own DecisionModel forward on MPS float32 vs CPU float32 for decider_stdio's warm-up (63 tokens) in four shapes (pad-to-64 with and without attention_mask, unpadded with and without); every decoder layer matched CPU to <4e-6 and the letter logits were identical (A 14.622, B 10.072, TIE 8.722) in all four (log logs/decider-bisect1.log). (2) The fault is decider/temperature.py scaled_softmax's list branch: t = torch.tensor(temperature, dtype=lg.dtype).to(lg.device, non_blocking=True). decider-2b v11's decider_config.json sets temperature_by_type (choice 1.164, noul 1.624, score 1.124), so every system_one call takes that branch. decider_mps_temp_check.py: scaled_softmax alone on MPS, 500 calls -> 500/500 NaN as shipped, 0/500 wrong with a synchronous .to(lg.device); Decider.system_one on MPS float32, 5 calls -> NaN every time as shipped, A 0.9743 / B 0.0195 / TIE 0.0061 every time (= CPU) with only that copy made synchronous (log logs/decider-tempcheck1.log). A non_blocking host-to-MPS copy from an unpinned, temporary tensor reads freed or not-yet-written memory, which explains every earlier symptom (NaN, flat 1/3, P=1.000, varying run to run). (3) Separately, decider.mps_ops.patch_mps returns False on transformers < 5.17 (this env has 5.12.1), so the MPS gated-delta patch never ran here; that is not the cause. The map path was introduced in decider-ai 1.4.0, so 1.3.x (scalar temperature) is unaffected. Workaround without editing the package: Decider(..., temperature=<scalar>) switches the by-type map off (TT.from_config), at the cost of the per-type calibration.

question: Does load_text_tower load a checkpoint whose output head is untied from the embedding (Qwen3.5-9B-Base: tie_word_embeddings false, lm_head.weight stored) as that model?
answer: No, before this fix: it loaded only model.language_model.* tensors, so lm_head.weight was dropped, and QwenDecisionStep trained the input embedding as the head, a different model, with nothing reporting it. ModelSpec.tied_embedding was never read. Fixed: qd_train.memory.head_is_tied decides the tie from the top-level config flag (the one transformers ties this architecture by), text_config's flag when stated, and the storage (an lm_head.* tensor), and refuses any disagreement or an absent top-level flag; load_text_tower refuses an untied head outright, and _verify_spec_describes compares tied_embedding along with every other architecture number. Tests: python/tests/test_backbone.py test_a_checkpoint_with_its_own_output_head_is_refused_not_silently_replaced, test_a_head_whose_tie_would_be_a_guess_is_refused_at_load, test_a_spec_wrong_about_any_architecture_number_is_refused. That each would have loaded silently before the fix is inferred from reading the old loader (it never read the tie, and compared four numbers), not run.
residual: Training an untied head is not built: the 9B is refused, not supported. A 9B run needs an untied-head path (the remap would cut two [V, H] matrices) and sharding (it fits no single card, HANDOFF/next-training-plan-2026-10-06.md section 4).
impact: A 9B run would have trained and reported a model whose head was not the checkpoint's.

question: Does the checkpoint-to-ModelSpec builder read the tie, the gate and the state dtype the checkpoint states?
answer: No, before this fix. memory_budget.spec_from_checkpoint read tie_word_embeddings from text_config with a default of false, so a 4B-shaped snapshot whose flag is top-level was read as untied; it defaulted attn_output_gate to false and the recurrent-state dtype to 2 bytes, read headers without a size bound, and accepted a config that says tied over a checkpoint storing a head. Measured on HEAD 8a531e8 with build/next-train-2026-10-06/prefix/prefix_4b.py: tied 4B read as tied_embedding=False; contradictory (tied + stored head) accepted. Fixed: the builder is qd_train.memory.spec_from_checkpoint, reads every field it needs or refuses (CheckpointRefused), decides the tie with head_is_tied, bounds the header read, refuses tensors under an unknown prefix, and checks embed_tokens' shape against the config. The 2B snapshot reproduces QWEN3_5_2B_TEXT field for field (python/tests/test_memory.py test_the_2b_snapshot_reproduces_the_2b_constant_field_for_field). memory_budget, gh200_rows and real_ft_run all call this one builder.
impact: A 4B budget would have been an untied budget, and the remap budget for it was wrong.

question: Can tools/real_ft_run.py budget and load any base other than the 2B?
answer: No, before this fix: _real_step called load_text_tower without spec=, so every backbone was described by QWEN3_5_2B_TEXT and any other base was refused at load by _verify_spec_describes. The only builder of a spec from a checkpoint lived in tools/memory_budget.py. Fixed: _real_step passes spec_from_checkpoint(backbone), refusing a snapshot the builder refuses as SystemExit. Test: python/tests/test_real_ft_device_budget.py test_the_real_step_budgets_the_base_on_disk_not_the_2b (fails before the fix: the load was given no spec).
impact: A 4B run could not start through the production path.

question: Does the memory model count a GDN layer whose value heads differ from its key heads (Qwen3.5-4B/9B-Base: 16 key, 32 value heads)?
answer: No, before this fix: ModelSpec had one linear head count, so qkv was 3 x key_dim, z and out_proj's input were hidden_size, and the recurrent state was key_heads x key_dim^2. On HEAD 8a531e8 a 4B-shaped spec gave 54,784 saved elements per linear layer per token and 1,048,576 recurrent-state bytes per row; the module's real widths give 64,000 and 2,097,152. Fixed: ModelSpec carries linear_value_heads and linear_value_head_dim (required, no default; a multiple of the key heads), the enumeration uses key_dim for q and k and value_dim for v, z, the norm and out_proj's input, and the recurrent state is [value_heads, key_dim, value_dim]. Checked against transformers' own Qwen3_5GatedDeltaNet at a 2:1 ratio, widths and a real recurrent state (test_backbone.py test_the_linear_layer_enumeration_uses_the_real_modules_widths_when_value_heads_differ). Every 2B figure is unchanged (test_memory.py test_the_2b_figures_are_unchanged_by_the_value_head_fields). Re-sized: AUDIT/next-train-2026-10-06/sizing.txt; 4B kahan on a GH200 still admits 38,552 tokens, H200 and B200 figures fell (4B kahan 125,294 -> 115,656 and 202,398 -> 192,760; 9B kahan B200 19,276 -> 9,638).
impact: The 4B and 9B budgets under-counted activations and the recurrent state, the direction that OOMs.

question: Is a run whose checkpoint MAX_SIDECAR_BYTES will refuse refused before it trains?
answer: No, before this fix: Checkpoint.write refused the sidecar at the first save, after the GPU time was spent. A 4B under master or kahan checkpoints 14 B/param, about 55 GiB, against the 32 GiB bound. Fixed in part: real_ft_run.checkpoint_sidecar_bytes computes the full checkpoint's tensor bytes from the built step (weights read off the modules, optimizer state as OptimizerSpec.checkpoint_bytes_per_param per optimized parameter) and refuses before step 0 when --checkpoint-every writes full checkpoints. The prediction equals the trained step's state() exactly on a tiny tower under master and kahan (test_backbone.py test_the_sidecar_preflight_predicts_the_checkpoint_the_step_writes); checkpoint_bytes_per_param is measured off each built optimizer's state_dict (test_optim.py test_each_recipe_checkpoints_the_bytes_its_spec_says). Also corrected: the bound's derivation said fp32 weights + moments (12 B/param) was the widest checkpoint; the master recipe (14) is wider; the bound still holds the 2B's widest (26,345,551,232 bytes, 1.30x headroom) and test_run_control.py now derives it over every built layout.
residual: The bound itself still refuses any 4B full checkpoint. It is a gate (rule 2): raising it for a larger base is the human's decision, and until then a 4B run cannot save a full checkpoint. P2 of the next plan writes none.
impact: A 4B run would have trained to its first save and lost its weights.

question: Can the row-capacity probe measure the next plan's P2 shape (the 4B under the kahan recipe, with the real loss head)?
answer: No, before this fix: the base, the recipe (plain bf16) and the widths were constants, and the backward was driven by hidden.pow(2).mean(), which never builds the loss head estimate_step budgets. Fixed: --snapshot (budgeted by spec_from_checkpoint), --optimizer (the specs real_ft_run builds under each name), --width, --loss {proxy,fused-ce} and --out; with no flags it runs what it always ran. Tests: python/tests/test_gh200_rows.py, including fused-ce giving every head row a gradient where the proxy does not, run on a tiny CPU tower through the same function the GPU probe calls.
impact: P2 had no instrument.

question: Does append_gap report a write that lands fewer bytes than the record?
answer: No, before this fix: os.write's return value was discarded. Reproduced on HEAD 8a531e8's gaps.py (build/next-train-2026-10-06/prefix/prefix_short_write.py): under a half write, append_gap returned normally and left 72 bytes with no trailing newline, a torn line that then blocks every later append through read_gaps. Fixed: a short write raises OSError naming the record, and is not retried (a second O_APPEND write could land after another lane's record and split this one around it). Test: python/tests/test_gaps_writer.py test_a_short_write_is_reported_not_swallowed.
impact: A torn gaps.jsonl line with no error at the point it was written.

question: Does estimate_step's loss-head term (an fp32 [V, H] accumulator plus one logit slab) match what the fused CE holds at the step's peak?
answer: Unmeasured. Read in code (DevMap audit #5): at the end of the CE forward the fp32 accumulator (counted) and its bf16 copy saved for backward (2VH bytes, not counted: 1.02 GB at the 2B, 1.27 GB at the 4B, 2.03 GB at the 9B) are both live, and grad_hidden [N, H] is not counted. Whether the copy lands on the step's global peak depends on allocator lifetimes. Every GH200 measurement so far (the 0.84-0.97x figure) drove a proxy loss and is backbone-only. The instrument now exists: tools/gh200_rows.py --loss fused-ce. The estimator is not changed before that measurement; the plan's 0.84 budget factor covers the backbone gap only.
impact: The step budget may under-count the loss head by up to 2VH bytes.

question: Does scoring a checkpoint (no gradient, no step) allocate and budget a training optimizer?
answer: Yes (DevMap audit #8). _scoring_step builds the training step: QwenDecisionStep constructs the optimizer, and device_budget checks the training footprint. Default fp32 scoring is budgeted as ADAMW_FP32 training (62.7 GiB at the 4B, 133.4 GiB at the 9B, where the fp32 weights alone are 33.4 GiB). MasterWeightAdamW clones fp32 masters at construction (4 B/param that scoring never uses: 7.0 GiB at the 2B). KahanBf16AdamW and torch AdamW now allocate at the first step (8a531e8), so under those a scoring step holds no optimizer state, but its budget still prices one. Fix: a scoring step with no optimizer and a scoring footprint (weights + no-grad activations + the logit slab).
impact: Scoring a 9B is refused on any single card; scoring under the master recipe holds 4 B/param it never uses.

question: Is every wait in the box queue bounded?
answer: No (DevMap audit #9, code read; the SIGKILL scenario inferred, not reproduced). wait_queued and after_early_j6f poll for a .done marker that an EXIT trap writes, with no deadline and no stop file; a SIGKILL (the OOM killer's included) runs no trap, so a waiter polls forever on an hourly-billed box. flock without -w blocks forever on a hung holder. v5_wait_marker is the bounded pattern (V5_HUMAN_WAIT_MAX_S, V5_STOP). The old queue is not edited: it ran and its box is gone. The v6 queue must bound every wait by the box budget (the box guard in HANDOFF/next-training-plan-2026-10-06.md precaution 4), use flock -w, and check the holder's pid.
impact: An unbounded wait is unbounded cost on a rented box.

question: Does the fused CE reduce over logits at the precision it states?
answer: No (DevMap audit #11, code read): with bf16 hidden and weight the per-chunk matmul's output is bf16 and only then upcast, so the fp32 logsumexp runs over logits already rounded to 8 mantissa bits (up to 0.0625 absolute at |logit| 16-32). Training is bf16 while scoring defaults to fp32, so the letter margins training optimises are not exactly the ones scored. Common practice (transformers' bf16 lm_head does the same). Not changed here: it is a numerics change, so it would make new rows incomparable to v5's, and its effect is unmeasured.
impact: Unmeasured; possibly a small train/score mismatch in letter margins.

question: Does the bf16 load keep the tensors the checkpoint stores in fp32?
answer: No (DevMap audit #12, header and code read): the 2B header stores 36 text tensors in F32 (linear_attn.A_log [16] and linear_attn.norm.weight [128] in each of 18 GDN layers) and the load rounds all of them to bf16; transformers 5.12.1 does the same (no _keep_in_fp32). Keeping them fp32 costs little (both optimizers treat fp32 parameters as their own masters) but changes numerics, so it is a recipe decision, and the release export would then have to choose their dtype explicitly.
impact: Small, inferred; unmeasured.

owner: the human (upstream report to github.com/Mapika/decider is his call)
finding: Root cause measured on this Mac (torch 2.12.1, transformers 5.12.1, M5 Pro), under tools/mac_heavy.sh. (1) The model is not at fault: decider_mps_bisect.py ran decider's own DecisionModel forward on MPS float32 vs CPU float32 for decider_stdio's warm-up (63 tokens) in four shapes (pad-to-64 with and without attention_mask, unpadded with and without); every decoder layer matched CPU to <4e-6 and the letter logits were identical (A 14.622, B 10.072, TIE 8.722) in all four (log logs/decider-bisect1.log). (2) The fault is decider/temperature.py scaled_softmax's list branch: t = torch.tensor(temperature, dtype=lg.dtype).to(lg.device, non_blocking=True). decider-2b v11's decider_config.json sets temperature_by_type (choice 1.164, noul 1.624, score 1.124), so every system_one call takes that branch. decider_mps_temp_check.py: scaled_softmax alone on MPS, 500 calls -> 500/500 NaN as shipped, 0/500 wrong with a synchronous .to(lg.device); Decider.system_one on MPS float32, 5 calls -> NaN every time as shipped, A 0.9743 / B 0.0195 / TIE 0.0061 every time (= CPU) with only that copy made synchronous (log logs/decider-tempcheck1.log). A non_blocking host-to-MPS copy from an unpinned, temporary tensor reads freed or not-yet-written memory, which explains every earlier symptom (NaN, flat 1/3, P=1.000, varying run to run). (3) Separately, decider.mps_ops.patch_mps returns False on transformers < 5.17 (this env has 5.12.1), so the MPS gated-delta patch never ran here; that is not the cause. The map path was introduced in decider-ai 1.4.0, so 1.3.x (scalar temperature) is unaffected. Workaround without editing the package: Decider(..., temperature=<scalar>) switches the by-type map off (TT.from_config), at the cost of the per-type calibration.

question: Were BKC and the _coop kernel naming retired on purpose or lost in a rename, and does the tile audit still pass having examined nothing?
answer: Neither retired nor renamed: the BKC check never applied to tessl. Over all 169 revisions (git log -S and git grep), no file under src/ defines COOP_BKC, none under kernels/ has constexpr int BKC, and no entry point (kernel void or *_KERNEL macro) carries a _coop suffix. COOP_BKC appears only in docs at 84a52a1, which commits no kernels, and in the script from d4e4f2d, where it arrived dead. It describes the blocked-K kernels of the code tessl was extracted from. Every tessl kernel passes K to matmul2d_descriptor as dynamic_length_v<int> and reduces it inside op.run(), so there is no K block to check. The BKC half was deleted. The _coop-keyed unpinned guard was replaced by a rule that every entry point is checked or exempt by name. Under the old script 10 of 27 entry points passed unexamined: bf16_f32 (template defaults), the f16 NN kernels x2, *_batched x3, split-K x3, and i8_f32. Now 26 are checked and i8_f32 is EXEMPT (nn.rs local SM/SN, not a TileGeom). Zero kernels, zero pairs, an unparseable *_KERNEL(, a stale pin or exemption, and an unreadable geometry all fail. PASS line on 2026-10-06: 'PASS: tile geometry: 26 kernels, 30 Rust dispatch pairs; 1 exempt (matmul2d_tensorops_i8_f32)'. The same result holds against HEAD's kernels/gemm.rs and the dirty working tree.

P1's val_gap needs per-row correctness for its paired bootstrap. --score-val alone writes only the eval row's val_top1.choice (correct/n); per-row results exist only when --verdicts-out PATH is also passed (write_verdicts_jsonl, kind/row_id/correct per val row). The DRAFT says '--score-val after each arm' and does not name --verdicts-out; the P1 queue must pass a distinct --verdicts-out per arm or the reading is refused. The DRAFT also leaves the bootstrap RNG and interval method unnamed; read_p1_parity fixes numpy default_rng(20261006), integers(0,n,size=n) per draw, percentile [2.5,97.5] linear, and states it in its output.

P1's 'optimizer step time (median of steps 101-600)' does not say whether it is optimizer.step() alone or the whole training step; real_ft_run now records both (train.optimizer_step_s, train.step_time_s) and read_p1_parity decides on the apply-alone one, reporting the other. 'measured peak ... at the same shape' names no shape or allocator figure: gh200_footprint sweeps 5 widths at 1 row with a proxy loss and full checkpointing (not the arm's recipe, not its fused CE or span head) and records max_memory_allocated; the reader requires the condition at every width and refuses on any OOM. Both choices need confirming in the pre-registration before the first P1 command.

The per-step time series could not go beside letter_log/span_log in the checkpoint: those live in QwenDecisionStep.state(), and load_state refuses any model_state key it does not write, so a key added from real_ft_run would break every resume. The ft row (tri-state metrics, scalar values only) carries the window's median plus min/p90/max and n/n_total; the series itself is held in memory only (<=500 floats per series). Persisting it needs a backbone.py change owned by another lane.

question: Does the v6 containment scan read the corpus a --v6-data-rules build writes?
answer: No (rg + code read, not graph-confirmed). containment_scan.py:622-624 builds under DataConfig().with_v6_benchmark_targets() only, never with_v6_dedupe_rules(), so its split is the lexical-keep split while a --v6-data-rules build splits by split priority behind the LSH prefilter; it names its corpus with benchmark_eval_splits_are_targets alone (:650-653). The pipeline and ft_splits now name a --v6-data-rules corpus with all three v6 fingerprint keys (real_tokenizer_pipeline.name_corpus), so an exclusion list from today's scan is refused by a v6 build (fail closed).
